1.0.oldText: Once, on a dark winter's day, when the yellow fog hung so thick and heavy in the streets of London that the lamps were lit and the shop windows blazed with gas as they do at night, an odd-looking little girl sat in a cab with her father and was driven rather slowly through the big streets.

1.1.oldText: She sat with her feet tucked under her, leaning against her father, who held her in his arm. She stared out of the window at the passing people with a strange, old-fashioned thoughtfulness in her big eyes.

1.2.oldText: She was such a little girl that you wouldn't expect to see such a look on her small face. It would have been an old look even for a child of twelve, and Sara Crewe was only seven. The fact was, however, that she was always dreaming and thinking strange things. She could not remember any time when she had not been thinking about grown-up people and the world they belonged to. She felt as if she had lived a long, long time.

1.3.oldText: At this moment she was remembering the voyage she had just made from Bombay with her father, Captain Crewe. She was thinking of the big ship, of the Lascars passing silently to and fro on it, of the children playing on the hot deck, and of some young officers' wives who used to try to make her talk to them and who laughed at the things she said.

1.4.oldText: Mostly, she was thinking what a strange thing it was that one moment you were in India in the blazing sun, and then in the middle of the ocean, and then driving in a strange vehicle through strange streets where the day was as dark as the night. She found this so puzzling that she moved closer to her father.

1.5.oldText: “Papa,” she said in a low, mysterious little voice that was almost a whisper, “papa.”

1.6.oldText: “What is it, darling?” Captain Crewe answered, holding her closer and looking down into her face. “What is Sara thinking of?”

1.7.oldText: “Is this the place?” Sara whispered, cuddling still closer to him. “Is it, papa?”

1.8.oldText: “Yes, little Sara, it is. We have reached it at last.” And though she was only seven years old, she knew that he felt sad when he said it.

1.9.oldText: It seemed to her many years since he had begun to prepare her mind for “the place,” as she always called it. Her mother had died when she was born, so she had never known her or missed her. Her young, handsome, rich, doting father seemed to be the only relation she had in the world. They had always played together and been fond of each other. She only knew he was rich because she had heard people say so when they thought she wasn't listening, and she had also heard them say that when she grew up she would be rich, too. She did not know all that being rich meant. She had always lived in a beautiful bungalow and was used to seeing many servants who bowed to her, called her “Missee Sahib,” and gave her her own way in everything. She had had toys and pets and an ayah who worshipped her, and she had gradually learned that people who were rich had these things. That, however, was all she knew about it.

1.10.oldText: During her short life only one thing had troubled her, and that thing was “the place” she was to be taken to one day. The climate of India was very bad for children, and as soon as possible they were sent away from it — usually to England and to school. She had seen other children go away, and had heard their fathers and mothers talk about the letters they received from them. She had known that she would have to go, too, and though sometimes her father's stories of the voyage and the new country had attracted her, she had been troubled by the thought that he could not stay with her.

1.11.oldText: “Couldn't you go to that place with me, papa?” she had asked when she was five years old. “Couldn't you go to school, too? I would help you with your lessons.”

1.12.oldText: “But you will not have to stay for a very long time, little Sara,” he had always said. “You will go to a nice house where there will be lots of little girls, and you will play together, and I will send you plenty of books. You will grow so fast that it will seem scarcely a year before you are big enough and clever enough to come back and take care of papa.”

1.13.oldText: She had liked to think of that. To keep house for her father; to ride with him, and sit at the head of his table when he had dinner parties; to talk to him and read his books — that would be what she would like most in the world. And if one had to go away to “the place” in England to achieve it, she must make up her mind to go. She did not care very much for other little girls, but if she had plenty of books she could console herself. She liked books more than anything else, and was, in fact, always inventing stories of beautiful things and telling them to herself. Sometimes she had told them to her father, and he had liked them as much as she did.

1.14.oldText: “Well, papa,” she said softly, “if we are here, I suppose we must be resigned.”

1.15.oldText: He laughed at her old-fashioned speech and kissed her. He was really not at all resigned himself, though he knew he must keep that a secret. His quaint little Sara had been a great companion to him, and he felt he would be a lonely man when, on his return to India, he went into his bungalow knowing he need not expect to see the small figure in its white dress come forward to meet him. So he held her very closely in his arms as the cab rolled into the big, dull square in which stood the house that was their destination.

1.16.oldText: It was a big, dull, brick house, exactly like all the others in its row, except that on the front door there shone a brass plate engraved in black letters:

1.19.oldText: “Here we are, Sara,” said Captain Crewe, making his voice sound as cheerful as possible. Then he lifted her out of the cab, and they climbed the steps and rang the bell. Sara often thought afterwards that the house was somehow exactly like Miss Minchin. It was respectable and well furnished, but everything in it was ugly; even the armchairs seemed to have hard bones in them. In the hall everything was hard and polished — even the red cheeks of the moon face on the tall clock in the corner had a severe, varnished look. The drawing room they were ushered into was covered by a carpet with a square pattern on it, the chairs were square, and a heavy marble clock stood upon the heavy marble mantel.

1.20.oldText: As she sat down in one of the stiff mahogany chairs, Sara cast one of her quick looks around her.

1.21.oldText: “I don't like it, papa,” she said. “But then I dare say soldiers — even brave ones — don't really LIKE going into battle.”

1.22.oldText: Captain Crewe laughed out loud at this. He was young and full of fun, and he never tired of hearing Sara's strange speeches.

1.23.oldText: “Oh, little Sara,” he said. “What shall I do when I have no one to say solemn things to me? No one else is as solemn as you are.”

1.24.oldText: “But why do solemn things make you laugh so?” asked Sara.

1.25.oldText: “Because you are such fun when you say them,” he answered, laughing still more. And then suddenly he swept her into his arms and kissed her very hard, stopping his laughter all at once and looking almost as if tears had come into his eyes.

1.26.oldText: It was just then that Miss Minchin entered the room. She was very like her house, Sara felt: tall and dull, and respectable and ugly. She had large, cold, fishy eyes, and a large, cold, fishy smile. It spread itself into a very large smile when she saw Sara and Captain Crewe. She had heard a great many desirable things of the young soldier from the lady who had recommended her school to him. Among other things, she had heard that he was a rich father willing to spend a great deal of money on his little daughter.

1.27.oldText: “It will be a great privilege to have charge of such a beautiful and promising child, Captain Crewe,” she said, taking Sara's hand and stroking it. “Lady Meredith has told me of her unusual cleverness. A clever child is a great treasure in an establishment like mine.”

1.28.oldText: Sara stood quietly, with her eyes fixed upon Miss Minchin's face. She was thinking something odd, as usual.

1.29.oldText: “Why does she say I am a beautiful child?” she was thinking. “I am not beautiful at all. Colonel Grange's little girl, Isobel, is beautiful. She has dimples and rose-colored cheeks, and long hair the color of gold. I have short black hair and green eyes; besides which, I am a thin child and not fair in the least. I am one of the ugliest children I have ever seen. She is beginning by telling a lie.”

1.30.oldText: She was mistaken, however, in thinking she was an ugly child. She was not in the least like Isobel Grange, who had been the beauty of the regiment, but she had an odd charm of her own. She was a slim, supple creature, rather tall for her age, with an intense, attractive little face. Her hair was thick and quite black and only curled at the tips; her eyes were greenish gray, it is true, but they were big, wonderful eyes with long, black lashes, and though she herself did not like the color of them, many other people did. Still, she was very firm in her belief that she was an ugly little girl, and she was not at all flattered by Miss Minchin's praise.

1.31.oldText: “I should be telling a lie if I said she was beautiful,” she thought; “and I should know I was telling a lie. I believe I am as ugly as she is — in my way. Why did she say that?”

1.32.oldText: After she had known Miss Minchin longer she learned why she had said it. She discovered that she said the same thing to every papa and mamma who brought a child to her school.

1.33.oldText: Sara stood near her father and listened while he and Miss Minchin talked. She had been brought to the seminary because Lady Meredith's two little girls had been educated there, and Captain Crewe had a great respect for Lady Meredith's experience. Sara was to be what was known as “a parlor boarder,” and she was to enjoy even greater privileges than parlor boarders usually did. She was to have a pretty bedroom and sitting room of her own; she was to have a pony and a carriage, and a maid to take the place of the ayah who had been her nurse in India.

1.34.oldText: “I am not in the least anxious about her education,” Captain Crewe said, with his cheerful laugh, as he held Sara's hand and patted it. “The difficulty will be to keep her from learning too fast and too much. She is always sitting with her little nose buried in books. She doesn't read them, Miss Minchin; she gobbles them up as if she were a little wolf instead of a little girl. She is always starving for new books to gobble, and she wants grown-up books — great, big, fat ones — French and German as well as English — history and biography and poets, and all sorts of things. Drag her away from her books when she reads too much. Make her ride her pony in the Row, or go out and buy a new doll. She ought to play more with dolls.”

1.35.oldText: “Papa,” said Sara, “you see, if I went out and bought a new doll every few days I should have more than I could be fond of. Dolls ought to be close friends. Emily is going to be my close friend.”

1.36.oldText: Captain Crewe looked at Miss Minchin and Miss Minchin looked at Captain Crewe.

1.38.oldText: “Tell her, Sara,” Captain Crewe said, smiling.

1.39.oldText: Sara's green-gray eyes looked very solemn and quite soft as she answered.

1.40.oldText: “She is a doll I haven't got yet,” she said. “She is a doll papa is going to buy for me. We are going out together to find her. I have called her Emily. She is going to be my friend when papa is gone. I want her to talk to about him.”

1.41.oldText: Miss Minchin's large, fishy smile became very flattering indeed.

1.42.oldText: “What an original child!” she said. “What a darling little creature!”

1.43.oldText: “Yes,” said Captain Crewe, drawing Sara close. “She is a darling little creature. Take great care of her for me, Miss Minchin.”

1.44.oldText: Sara stayed with her father at his hotel for several days; in fact, she remained with him until he sailed away again to India. They went out and visited many big shops together and bought a great many things. They bought, in fact, a great many more things than Sara needed; but Captain Crewe was a rash, innocent young man and wanted his little girl to have everything she admired and everything he admired himself. So between them they collected a wardrobe much too grand for a child of seven. There were velvet dresses trimmed with costly furs, lace dresses, embroidered dresses, hats with great soft ostrich feathers, ermine coats and muffs, and boxes of tiny gloves and handkerchiefs and silk stockings in such abundant supplies that the polite young women behind the counters whispered to each other that the odd little girl with the big, solemn eyes must be at least some foreign princess — perhaps the little daughter of an Indian rajah.

1.45.oldText: And at last they found Emily, but they went to a number of toy shops and looked at a great many dolls before they discovered her.

1.46.oldText: “I want her to look as if she wasn't really a doll,” Sara said. “I want her to look as if she LISTENS when I talk to her. The trouble with dolls, papa” — and she put her head on one side and reflected as she said it — “the trouble with dolls is that they never seem to HEAR.” So they looked at big ones and little ones — at dolls with black eyes and dolls with blue — at dolls with brown curls and dolls with golden braids, dolls dressed and dolls undressed.

1.47.oldText: “You see,” Sara said when they were examining one who had no clothes. “If, when I find her, she has no dresses, we can take her to a dressmaker and have her things made to fit. They will fit better if they are tried on.”

1.48.oldText: After a number of disappointments they decided to walk and look in at the shop windows and let the cab follow them. They had passed two or three places without even going in, when, as they were approaching a shop that was really not a very large one, Sara suddenly started and clutched her father's arm.

1.50.oldText: A flush had risen to her face, and there was an expression in her green-gray eyes as if she had just recognized someone she was close to and fond of.

1.51.oldText: “She is actually waiting there for us!” she said. “Let us go in to her.”

1.52.oldText: “Dear me,” said Captain Crewe, “I feel as if we ought to have someone to introduce us.”

1.53.oldText: “You must introduce me and I will introduce you,” said Sara. “But I knew her the minute I saw her — so perhaps she knew me, too.”

1.54.oldText: Perhaps she had known her. She certainly had a very intelligent expression in her eyes when Sara took her in her arms. She was a large doll, but not too large to carry about easily; she had naturally curling golden-brown hair, which hung like a cloak around her, and her eyes were a deep, clear, gray-blue, with soft, thick eyelashes that were real eyelashes and not mere painted lines.

1.55.oldText: “Of course,” said Sara, looking into her face as she held her on her knee, “of course, papa, this is Emily.”

1.56.oldText: So Emily was bought and actually taken to a children's outfitter's shop and measured for a wardrobe as grand as Sara's own. She had lace dresses, too, and velvet and muslin ones, and hats and coats and beautiful lace-trimmed underclothes, and gloves and handkerchiefs and furs.

1.57.oldText: “I should like her always to look as if she was a child with a good mother,” said Sara. “I'm her mother, though I am going to make a companion of her.”

1.58.oldText: Captain Crewe would really have enjoyed the shopping enormously, except that a sad thought kept tugging at his heart. All this meant that he was going to be separated from his beloved, quaint little companion.

1.59.oldText: He got out of his bed in the middle of that night and went and stood looking down at Sara, who lay asleep with Emily in her arms. Her black hair was spread out on the pillow and Emily's golden-brown hair mingled with it. Both of them had lace-ruffled nightgowns, and both had long eyelashes that lay and curled up on their cheeks. Emily looked so like a real child that Captain Crewe felt glad she was there. He drew a big sigh and pulled his mustache with a boyish expression.

1.60.oldText: “Heigh-ho, little Sara!” he said to himself. “I don't believe you know how much your daddy will miss you.”

1.61.oldText: The next day he took her to Miss Minchin's and left her there. He was to sail away the next morning. He explained to Miss Minchin that his lawyers, Messrs. Barrow & Skipworth, had charge of his affairs in England and would give her any advice she wanted, and that they would pay the bills she sent in for Sara's expenses. He would write to Sara twice a week, and she was to be given every pleasure she asked for.

1.62.oldText: “She is a sensible little thing, and she never wants anything that isn't safe to give her,” he said.

1.63.oldText: Then he went with Sara into her little sitting room and they said goodbye to each other. Sara sat on his knee and held the lapels of his coat in her small hands, and looked long and hard at his face.

1.64.oldText: “Are you learning me by heart, little Sara?” he said, stroking her hair.

1.65.oldText: “No,” she answered. “I know you by heart. You are inside my heart.” And they put their arms around each other and kissed as if they would never let each other go.

1.66.oldText: When the cab drove away from the door, Sara was sitting on the floor of her sitting room, with her hands under her chin and her eyes following it until it had turned the corner of the square. Emily was sitting beside her, and she looked after it, too. When Miss Minchin sent her sister, Miss Amelia, to see what the child was doing, she found she could not open the door.

1.67.oldText: “I have locked it,” said a strange, polite little voice from inside. “I want to be quite by myself, if you please.”

1.68.oldText: Miss Amelia was fat and dumpy, and stood very much in awe of her sister. She was really the better-natured person of the two, but she never disobeyed Miss Minchin. She went downstairs again, looking almost alarmed.

1.69.oldText: “I never saw such a funny, old-fashioned child, sister,” she said. “She has locked herself in, and she is not making the slightest bit of noise.”

1.70.oldText: “It is much better than if she kicked and screamed, as some of them do,” Miss Minchin answered. “I expected that a child as spoiled as she is would set the whole house in an uproar. If ever a child was given her own way in everything, she is.”

1.71.oldText: “I've been opening her trunks and putting her things away,” said Miss Amelia. “I never saw anything like them — sable and ermine on her coats, and real Valenciennes lace on her underclothes. You have seen some of her clothes. What DO you think of them?”

1.72.oldText: “I think they are perfectly ridiculous,” replied Miss Minchin sharply; “but they will look very well at the head of the line when we take the schoolchildren to church on Sunday. She has been provided for as if she were a little princess.”

1.73.oldText: And upstairs in the locked room Sara and Emily sat on the floor and stared at the corner round which the cab had disappeared, while Captain Crewe looked backward, waving and kissing his hand as if he could not bear to stop.

2.0.oldText: When Sara entered the schoolroom the next morning, everybody looked at her with wide, interested eyes. By that time every pupil — from Lavinia Herbert, who was nearly thirteen and felt quite grown up, to Lottie Legh, who was only just four and the baby of the school — had heard a great deal about her. They knew very certainly that she was Miss Minchin's show pupil and was considered a credit to the establishment. One or two of them had even caught a glimpse of her French maid, Mariette, who had arrived the evening before. Lavinia had managed to pass Sara's room when the door was open, and had seen Mariette opening a box that had arrived late from some shop.

2.1.oldText: “It was full of petticoats with lace frills on them — frills and frills,” she whispered to her friend Jessie as she bent over her geography. “I saw her shaking them out. I heard Miss Minchin say to Miss Amelia that her clothes were so grand that they were ridiculous for a child. My mamma says that children should be dressed simply. She has got one of those petticoats on now. I saw it when she sat down.”

2.2.oldText: “She has silk stockings on!” whispered Jessie, also bending over her geography. “And what little feet! I never saw such little feet.”

2.3.oldText: “Oh,” sniffed Lavinia spitefully, “that is the way her slippers are made. My mamma says that even big feet can be made to look small if you have a clever shoemaker. I don't think she is pretty at all. Her eyes are such a strange color.”

2.4.oldText: “She isn't pretty the way other pretty people are,” said Jessie, stealing a glance across the room; “but she makes you want to look at her again. She has tremendously long eyelashes, but her eyes are almost green.”

2.5.oldText: Sara was sitting quietly in her seat, waiting to be told what to do. She had been placed near Miss Minchin's desk. She was not embarrassed at all by the many pairs of eyes watching her. She was interested and looked back quietly at the children who looked at her. She wondered what they were thinking of, and whether they liked Miss Minchin, and whether they cared for their lessons, and whether any of them had a papa at all like her own. She had had a long talk with Emily about her papa that morning.

2.6.oldText: “He is on the sea now, Emily,” she had said. “We must be very great friends to each other and tell each other things. Emily, look at me. You have the nicest eyes I ever saw — but I wish you could speak.”

2.7.oldText: She was a child full of imaginings and whimsical thoughts, and one of her fancies was that there would be a great deal of comfort in even pretending that Emily was alive and really heard and understood. After Mariette had dressed her in her dark-blue schoolroom dress and tied her hair with a dark-blue ribbon, she went to Emily, who sat in a chair of her own, and gave her a book.

2.8.oldText: “You can read that while I am downstairs,” she said; and, seeing Mariette looking at her curiously, she spoke to her with a serious little face.

2.9.oldText: “What I believe about dolls,” she said, “is that they can do things they will not let us know about. Perhaps, really, Emily can read and talk and walk, but she will only do it when people are out of the room. That is her secret. You see, if people knew that dolls could do things, they would make them work. So perhaps they have promised each other to keep it a secret. If you stay in the room, Emily will just sit there and stare; but if you go out, she will begin to read, perhaps, or go and look out of the window. Then if she heard either of us coming, she would just run back and jump into her chair and pretend she had been there the whole time.”

2.10.oldText: “Comme elle est drole!” Mariette said to herself, and when she went downstairs she told the head housemaid about it. But she had already begun to like this odd little girl who had such an intelligent small face and such perfect manners. She had taken care of children before who were not so polite. Sara was a very fine little person, and had a gentle, appreciative way of saying, “If you please, Mariette,” “Thank you, Mariette,” which was very charming. Mariette told the head housemaid that she thanked her as if she was thanking a lady.

2.11.oldText: “Elle a l'air d'une princesse, cette petite,” she said. Indeed, she was very pleased with her new little mistress and liked her position greatly.

2.12.oldText: After Sara had sat in her seat in the schoolroom for a few minutes, being looked at by the pupils, Miss Minchin rapped in a dignified manner upon her desk.

2.13.oldText: “Young ladies,” she said, “I wish to introduce you to your new companion.” All the little girls rose in their places, and Sara rose also. “I shall expect you all to be very pleasant to Miss Crewe; she has just come to us from a great distance — in fact, from India. As soon as lessons are over you must get to know each other.”

2.14.oldText: The pupils bowed ceremoniously, and Sara made a little curtsy, and then they sat down and looked at each other again.

2.15.oldText: “Sara,” said Miss Minchin in her schoolroom manner, “come here to me.”

2.16.oldText: She had taken a book from the desk and was turning over its pages. Sara went to her politely.

2.17.oldText: “As your papa has hired a French maid for you,” she began, “I conclude that he wishes you to make a special study of the French language.”

2.19.oldText: “I think he hired her,” she said, “because he — he thought I would like her, Miss Minchin.”

2.20.oldText: “I am afraid,” said Miss Minchin, with a slightly sour smile, “that you have been a very spoiled little girl and always imagine that things are done because you like them. My impression is that your papa wished you to learn French.”

2.21.oldText: If Sara had been older or less particular about being quite polite to people, she could have explained herself in a very few words. But, as it was, she felt a flush rising in her cheeks. Miss Minchin was a very severe and imposing person, and she seemed so absolutely sure that Sara knew nothing whatever of French that she felt as if it would be almost rude to correct her. The truth was that Sara could not remember a time when she had not seemed to know French. Her father had often spoken it to her when she had been a baby. Her mother had been a French woman, and Captain Crewe had loved her language, so it happened that Sara had always heard it and been familiar with it.

2.22.oldText: “I — I have never really learned French, but — but —” she began, trying shyly to make herself clear.

2.23.oldText: One of Miss Minchin's chief secret annoyances was that she did not speak French herself, and was eager to hide the irritating fact. She, therefore, had no intention of discussing the matter and laying herself open to innocent questioning by a new little pupil.

2.24.oldText: “That is enough,” she said with polite tartness. “If you have not learned, you must begin at once. The French master, Monsieur Dufarge, will be here in a few minutes. Take this book and look at it until he arrives.”

2.25.oldText: Sara's cheeks felt warm. She went back to her seat and opened the book. She looked at the first page with a serious face. She knew it would be rude to smile, and she was very determined not to be rude. But it was very strange to find herself expected to study a page that told her that “le pere” meant “the father,” and “la mere” meant “the mother.”

2.26.oldText: Miss Minchin glanced toward her searchingly.

2.27.oldText: “You look rather cross, Sara,” she said. “I am sorry you do not like the idea of learning French.”

2.28.oldText: “I am very fond of it,” answered Sara, thinking she would try again; “but —”

2.29.oldText: “You must not say ‘but’ when you are told to do things,” said Miss Minchin. “Look at your book again.”

2.30.oldText: And Sara did so, and did not smile, even when she found that “le fils” meant “the son,” and “le frere” meant “the brother.”

2.31.oldText: “When Monsieur Dufarge comes,” she thought, “I can make him understand.”

2.32.oldText: Monsieur Dufarge arrived very shortly afterward. He was a very nice, intelligent, middle-aged Frenchman, and he looked interested when his eyes fell upon Sara trying politely to seem absorbed in her little book of phrases.

2.33.oldText: “Is this a new pupil for me, madame?” he said to Miss Minchin. “I hope that is my good fortune.”

2.34.oldText: “Her papa — Captain Crewe — is very anxious that she should begin the language. But I am afraid she has a childish prejudice against it. She does not seem to wish to learn,” said Miss Minchin.

2.35.oldText: “I am sorry to hear that, mademoiselle,” he said kindly to Sara. “Perhaps, when we begin to study together, I may show you that it is a charming language.”

2.36.oldText: Little Sara rose in her seat. She was beginning to feel rather desperate, as if she were almost in disgrace. She looked up into Monsieur Dufarge's face with her big, green-gray eyes, and they were quite innocently appealing. She knew that he would understand as soon as she spoke. She began to explain quite simply in pretty and fluent French. Madame had not understood. She had not learned French exactly — not out of books — but her papa and other people had always spoken it to her, and she had read it and written it as she had read and written English. Her papa loved it, and she loved it because he did. Her dear mamma, who had died when she was born, had been French. She would be glad to learn anything monsieur would teach her, but what she had tried to explain to madame was that she already knew the words in this book — and she held out the little book of phrases.

2.37.oldText: When she began to speak Miss Minchin started quite violently and sat staring at her over her eyeglasses, almost indignantly, until she had finished. Monsieur Dufarge began to smile, and his smile was one of great pleasure. To hear this pretty childish voice speaking his own language so simply and charmingly made him feel almost as if he were in his native land — which on dark, foggy days in London sometimes seemed worlds away. When she had finished, he took the phrase book from her with a look almost affectionate. But he spoke to Miss Minchin.

2.38.oldText: “Ah, madame,” he said, “there is not much I can teach her. She has not LEARNED French; she is French. Her accent is exquisite.”

2.39.oldText: “You ought to have told me,” exclaimed Miss Minchin, much mortified, turning to Sara.

2.40.oldText: “I — I tried,” said Sara. “I — I suppose I did not begin right.”

2.41.oldText: Miss Minchin knew she had tried, and that it had not been her fault that she was not allowed to explain. And when she saw that the pupils had been listening and that Lavinia and Jessie were giggling behind their French grammars, she felt furious.

2.42.oldText: “Silence, young ladies!” she said severely, rapping upon the desk. “Silence at once!”

2.43.oldText: And from that minute on she began to feel rather a grudge against her show pupil.

4.0.oldText: If Sara had been a different kind of child, the life she led at Miss Minchin's Select Seminary for the next few years would not have been at all good for her. She was treated more as if she were a distinguished guest at the establishment than as if she were just a little girl. If she had been a self-important, domineering child, she might have become disagreeable enough to be unbearable from being so indulged and flattered. If she had been a lazy child, she would have learned nothing. Privately, Miss Minchin disliked her, but she was far too worldly a woman to do or say anything that might make such a desirable pupil wish to leave her school. She knew quite well that if Sara wrote to her papa to say she was uncomfortable or unhappy, Captain Crewe would remove her at once. Miss Minchin's opinion was that if a child were continually praised and never forbidden to do what she liked, she was sure to grow fond of the place where she was treated this way. Accordingly, Sara was praised for her quickness at her lessons, for her good manners, for her kindness to her fellow pupils, for her generosity if she gave sixpence to a beggar from her full little purse. The simplest thing she did was treated as if it were a virtue, and if she had not had a real disposition and a clever little brain, she might have become a very self-satisfied young person. But the clever little brain told her a great many sensible and true things about herself and her circumstances, and now and then she talked these things over with Ermengarde as time went on.

4.1.oldText: “Things happen to people by accident,” she used to say. “A lot of nice accidents have happened to me. It just HAPPENED that I always liked lessons and books, and could remember things when I learned them. It just happened that I was born with a father who was beautiful and nice and clever, and could give me everything I liked. Perhaps I really don't have a good temper at all, but if you have everything you want and everyone is kind to you, how can you help being good-tempered? I don't know” — looking quite serious — “how I shall ever find out whether I am really a nice child or a horrid one. Perhaps I'm a HIDEOUS child, and no one will ever know, just because I never have any trials.”

4.2.oldText: “Lavinia has no trials,” said Ermengarde, stolidly, “and she is horrid enough.”

4.3.oldText: Sara rubbed the end of her little nose thoughtfully, as she thought the matter over.

4.4.oldText: “Well,” she said at last, “perhaps — perhaps that is because Lavinia is GROWING.” This was the result of kindly remembering that Miss Amelia had said Lavinia was growing so fast she believed it affected her health and temper.

4.5.oldText: Lavinia was, in fact, spiteful. She was extremely jealous of Sara. Until the new pupil's arrival, she had felt herself the leader of the school. She had led because she was capable of making herself extremely disagreeable if the others did not follow her. She bullied the little children, and put on grand airs with those big enough to be her companions. She was rather pretty, and had been the best-dressed pupil in the procession when the Select Seminary walked out two by two, until Sara's velvet coats and sable muffs appeared, combined with drooping ostrich feathers, and were led by Miss Minchin at the head of the line. This, at the start, had been bitter enough; but as time went on it became clear that Sara was a leader too — and not because she could make herself disagreeable, but because she never did.

4.6.oldText: “There's one thing about Sara Crewe,” Jessie had once said, infuriating her “best friend” with her honesty. “She's never ‘grand’ about herself the least bit, and you know she might be, Lavvie. I believe I couldn't help being — just a little — if I had so many fine things and was made such a fuss over. It's disgusting, the way Miss Minchin shows her off when parents come.”

4.7.oldText: “‘Dear Sara must come into the drawing room and talk to Mrs. Musgrave about India,’” mimicked Lavinia, in her most exaggerated imitation of Miss Minchin. “‘Dear Sara must speak French to Lady Pitkin. Her accent is so perfect.’ Well, she didn't learn her French at the seminary, anyway. And there's nothing so clever in her knowing it. She says herself she didn't learn it at all. She just picked it up because she always heard her papa speak it. And as for her papa, there is nothing so grand in being an Indian officer.”

4.8.oldText: “Well,” said Jessie, slowly, “he's killed tigers. He killed the one in the skin Sara has in her room. That's why she likes it so. She lies on it and strokes its head, and talks to it as if it were a cat.”

4.9.oldText: “She's always doing something silly,” snapped Lavinia. “My mamma says that way of hers of pretending things is silly. She says she will grow up eccentric.”

4.10.oldText: It was quite true that Sara was never “grand.” She was a friendly little soul, and shared her privileges and belongings freely. The little ones, who were used to being looked down on and ordered out of the way by mature ladies of ten and twelve, were never made to cry by this most envied of them all. She was a motherly young person, and when people fell down and scraped their knees, she ran and helped them up and patted them, or found in her pocket a bonbon or some other soothing item. She never pushed them out of her way or treated their young years as a humiliation and a stain on their small characters.

4.11.oldText: “If you are four, you are four,” she said sternly to Lavinia on an occasion when Lavinia had — it must be confessed — slapped Lottie and called her “a brat.” “But you will be five next year, and six the year after that. And,” opening large, accusing eyes, “it takes sixteen years to make you twenty.”

4.12.oldText: “Dear me,” said Lavinia, “how we can calculate!” Indeed, it could not be denied that sixteen and four made twenty — and twenty was an age the most daring were scarcely bold enough to dream of.

4.13.oldText: So the younger children adored Sara. More than once she had been known to hold a tea party, made up of these despised little ones, in her own room. And Emily had been played with, and Emily's own tea service used — the one with cups that held quite a lot of much-sweetened weak tea and had blue flowers on them. No one had seen such a real-looking doll's tea set before. From that afternoon, Sara was regarded as a goddess and a queen by the entire alphabet class.

4.14.oldText: Lottie Legh worshipped her to such an extent that if Sara had not been a motherly person, she would have found her tiresome. Lottie had been sent to school by a rather flighty young papa who could not imagine what else to do with her. Her young mother had died, and as the child had been treated like a favorite doll or a very spoiled pet monkey or lap dog ever since the first hour of her life, she was a very alarming little creature. When she wanted anything or did not want anything, she wept and howled. And, as she always wanted the things she could not have, and did not want the things that were best for her, her shrill little voice was usually to be heard wailing in one part of the house or another.

4.15.oldText: Her strongest weapon was that, in some mysterious way, she had figured out that a very small girl who had lost her mother was a person who ought to be pitied and made much of. She had probably heard some grown-up people talking about her in the early days, after her mother's death. So it became her habit to make great use of this knowledge.

4.16.oldText: The first time Sara took her in charge was one morning when, walking past a sitting room, she heard both Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia trying to suppress the angry wails of some child who, evidently, refused to be silenced. She refused so violently, in fact, that Miss Minchin was forced to almost shout — in a stately and severe manner — to make herself heard.

4.17.oldText: “What IS she crying for?” she almost yelled.

4.18.oldText: “Oh — oh — oh!” Sara heard. “I haven't got any mam — ma-a!”

4.19.oldText: “Oh, Lottie!” screamed Miss Amelia. “Do stop, darling! Don't cry! Please don't!”

4.20.oldText: “Oh! Oh! Oh! Oh! Oh!” Lottie howled stormily. “Haven't — got — any — mam — ma-a!”

4.21.oldText: “She ought to be whipped,” Miss Minchin proclaimed. “You SHALL be whipped, you naughty child!”

4.22.oldText: Lottie wailed more loudly than ever. Miss Amelia began to cry. Miss Minchin's voice rose until it almost thundered, then suddenly she sprang up from her chair in helpless fury and stormed out of the room, leaving Miss Amelia to sort the matter out.

4.23.oldText: Sara had paused in the hall, wondering whether she ought to go into the room, because she had recently begun a friendly acquaintance with Lottie and might be able to quiet her. When Miss Minchin came out and saw her, she looked rather annoyed. She realized that her voice, as heard from inside the room, could not have sounded either dignified or kind.

4.24.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” she exclaimed, trying to produce a suitable smile.

4.25.oldText: “I stopped,” explained Sara, “because I knew it was Lottie — and I thought, perhaps — just perhaps, I could make her be quiet. May I try, Miss Minchin?”

4.26.oldText: “If you can, you are a clever child,” answered Miss Minchin, drawing in her mouth sharply. Then, seeing that Sara looked slightly chilled by her sharpness, she changed her manner. “But you are clever in everything,” she said in her approving way. “I dare say you can manage her. Go in.” And she left her.

4.27.oldText: When Sara entered the room, Lottie was lying on the floor, screaming and kicking her small fat legs violently, and Miss Amelia was bending over her in alarm and despair, looking quite red and damp with heat. Lottie had always found, in her own nursery at home, that kicking and screaming would always get her quieted by whatever means she insisted on. Poor plump Miss Amelia was trying first one method, and then another.

4.28.oldText: “Poor darling,” she said one moment. “I know you haven't any mamma, poor —” Then in quite another tone, “If you don't stop, Lottie, I will shake you. Poor little angel! There —! You wicked, bad, detestable child, I will smack you! I will!”

4.29.oldText: Sara went to them quietly. She did not know at all what she was going to do, but she had a vague inner conviction that it would be better not to say such different kinds of things quite so helplessly and excitedly.

4.30.oldText: “Miss Amelia,” she said in a low voice, “Miss Minchin says I may try to make her stop — may I?”

4.31.oldText: Miss Amelia turned and looked at her hopelessly. “Oh, DO you think you can?” she gasped.

4.32.oldText: “I don't know whether I CAN,” answered Sara, still in her half-whisper, “but I will try.”

4.33.oldText: Miss Amelia stumbled up from her knees with a heavy sigh, and Lottie's fat little legs kicked as hard as ever.

4.34.oldText: “If you will slip out of the room,” said Sara, “I will stay with her.”

4.35.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” Miss Amelia almost whimpered. “We never had such a dreadful child before. I don't believe we can keep her.”

4.36.oldText: But she crept out of the room, very much relieved to find an excuse for doing it.

4.37.oldText: Sara stood by the howling, furious child for a few moments, looking down at her without saying anything. Then she sat down flat on the floor beside her and waited. Except for Lottie's angry screams, the room was quite quiet. This was a new state of affairs for little Miss Legh, who was used to hearing other people protest and beg and command and coax by turns when she screamed. To lie and kick and shriek, and find the only person near you not seeming to mind in the least, caught her attention. She opened her tightly shut, streaming eyes to see who this person was. And it was only another little girl. But it was the one who owned Emily and all the nice things. And she was looking at her steadily, as if she was simply thinking. Having paused for a few seconds to figure this out, Lottie thought she had better start again, but the quiet of the room and Sara's odd, interested face made her first howl rather half-hearted.

4.38.oldText: “I — haven't — any — ma — ma — ma-a!” she announced; but her voice was not so strong.

4.39.oldText: Sara looked at her even more steadily, but with a sort of understanding in her eyes.

4.41.oldText: This was so unexpected that it was astonishing. Lottie actually dropped her legs, gave a wriggle, and lay there staring. A new idea will stop a crying child when nothing else will. Also, it was true that while Lottie disliked Miss Minchin, who was cross, and Miss Amelia, who was foolishly indulgent, she rather liked Sara, little as she knew her. She did not want to give up her grievance, but her thoughts were distracted from it. So she wriggled again, and after a sulky sob, said, “Where is she?”

4.42.oldText: Sara paused a moment. Because she had been told that her mamma was in heaven, she had thought a great deal about the matter, and her thoughts had not been quite like those of other people.

4.43.oldText: “She went to heaven,” she said. “But I am sure she comes out sometimes to see me — though I don't see her. So does yours. Perhaps they can both see us now. Perhaps they are both in this room.”

4.44.oldText: Lottie sat bolt upright and looked about her. She was a pretty, little, curly-headed creature, and her round eyes were like wet forget-me-nots. If her mamma had seen her during the last half-hour, she might not have thought her the kind of child who ought to be related to an angel.

4.45.oldText: Sara went on talking. Perhaps some people might think what she said was rather like a fairy story, but it was all so real to her own imagination that Lottie began to listen in spite of herself. She had been told that her mamma had wings and a crown, and she had been shown pictures of ladies in beautiful white nightgowns who were said to be angels. But Sara seemed to be telling a real story about a lovely country where real people were.

4.46.oldText: “There are fields and fields of flowers,” she said, forgetting herself, as usual, when she began, and talking rather as if she were in a dream. “Fields and fields of lilies — and when the soft wind blows over them, it carries the scent of them into the air — and everybody always breathes it, because the soft wind is always blowing. And little children run about in the lily fields and gather armfuls of them, and laugh and make little wreaths. And the streets are shining. And people are never tired, however far they walk. They can float anywhere they like. And there are walls made of pearl and gold all around the city, but they are low enough for the people to go and lean on them, and look down onto the earth and smile, and send beautiful messages.”

4.47.oldText: Whatever story she had begun to tell, Lottie would, no doubt, have stopped crying and been fascinated into listening. But there was no denying that this story was prettier than most others. She dragged herself close to Sara, and drank in every word until the end came — far too soon. When it did come, she was so sorry that she stuck out her lip ominously.

4.48.oldText: “I want to go there,” she cried. “I — haven't any mamma in this school.”

4.49.oldText: Sara saw the danger signal and came out of her dream. She took hold of the chubby hand and pulled her close to her side with a coaxing little laugh.

4.50.oldText: “I will be your mamma,” she said. “We will play that you are my little girl. And Emily shall be your sister.”

4.51.oldText: Lottie's dimples all began to show themselves.

4.53.oldText: “Yes,” answered Sara, jumping to her feet. “Let's go and tell her. And then I will wash your face and brush your hair.”

4.54.oldText: Lottie agreed quite cheerfully, and trotted out of the room and upstairs with her, without seeming even to remember that the whole of the last hour's tragedy had been caused by the fact that she had refused to be washed and brushed for lunch, and Miss Minchin had been called in to use her majestic authority.

4.55.oldText: And from that time on, Sara was an adopted mother.

9.0.oldText: The third person in the trio was Lottie. She was a small thing and did not know what hardship meant, and she was very confused by the change she saw in her young adopted mother. She had heard rumors that strange things had happened to Sara, but she could not understand why she looked different — why she wore an old black dress and came into the schoolroom only to teach instead of sitting in her place of honor and learning lessons herself. There had been much whispering among the little ones when they had discovered that Sara no longer lived in the rooms where Emily had so long sat in state. Lottie's biggest problem was that Sara said so little when one asked her questions. At seven, mysteries must be made very clear if you are to understand them.

9.1.oldText: “Are you very poor now, Sara?” she had asked privately the first morning her friend took charge of the small French class. “Are you as poor as a beggar?” She thrust a fat hand into the slim one and opened round, tearful eyes. “I don't want you to be as poor as a beggar.”

9.2.oldText: She looked as if she were about to cry. Sara hurriedly comforted her.

9.3.oldText: “Beggars have nowhere to live,” she said bravely. “I have a place to live in.”

9.4.oldText: “Where do you live?” Lottie persisted. “The new girl sleeps in your room, and it isn't pretty any more.”

9.5.oldText: “I live in another room,” said Sara.

9.6.oldText: “Is it a nice one?” Lottie asked. “I want to go and see it.”

9.7.oldText: “You must not talk,” said Sara. “Miss Minchin is looking at us. She will be angry with me for letting you whisper.”

9.8.oldText: She had already discovered that she was held responsible for everything that anyone objected to. If the children were not paying attention, if they talked, if they were restless, she was the one who would be scolded.

9.9.oldText: But Lottie was a determined little person. If Sara would not tell her where she lived, she would find out some other way. She talked to her small companions, hung around the older girls, and listened when they were gossiping. Acting on certain bits of information they had unconsciously let slip, she set off late one afternoon on a voyage of discovery, climbing stairs she had never known existed, until she reached the attic floor. There she found two doors near each other, and opening one of them, she saw her beloved Sara standing on an old table and looking out a window.

9.10.oldText: “Sara!” she cried, horrified. “Mamma Sara!” She was horrified because the attic was so bare and ugly and seemed so far away from the rest of the world. Her short legs had felt as if they had climbed hundreds of stairs.

9.11.oldText: Sara turned at the sound of her voice. It was her turn to be horrified. What would happen now? If Lottie began to cry and anyone happened to hear, they were both lost. She jumped down from her table and ran to the child.

9.12.oldText: “Don't cry and make a noise,” she begged. “I'll be scolded if you do, and I have been scolded all day. It's — it's not such a bad room, Lottie.”

9.13.oldText: “Isn't it?” Lottie gasped, and as she looked round it she bit her lip. She was still a spoiled child, but she was fond enough of her adopted mother to make an effort to control herself for her sake. Then somehow it was quite possible that any place Sara lived in might turn out to be nice. “Why isn't it, Sara?” she almost whispered.

9.14.oldText: Sara hugged her close and tried to laugh. There was a sort of comfort in the warmth of the plump little body. She had had a hard day and had been staring out of the windows with hot eyes.

9.15.oldText: “You can see all sorts of things you can't see downstairs,” she said.

9.16.oldText: “What sort of things?” demanded Lottie, with that curiosity Sara could always wake up even in bigger girls.

9.17.oldText: “Chimneys — quite close to us — with smoke curling up in wreaths and clouds and going up into the sky — and sparrows hopping about and talking to each other just as if they were people — and other attic windows where heads might pop out any minute, and you can wonder who they belong to. And it all feels so high up — as if it were another world.”

9.18.oldText: “Oh, let me see it!” cried Lottie. “Lift me up!”

9.19.oldText: Sara lifted her up, and they stood on the old table together and leaned on the edge of the flat window in the roof, and looked out.

9.20.oldText: Anyone who has not done this does not know what a different world they saw. The slates spread out on either side of them and slanted down into the rain gutters. The sparrows, being at home up there, twittered and hopped about quite without fear. Two of them perched on the nearest chimney top and quarreled fiercely until one pecked the other and drove him away. The garret window next to theirs was shut, because the house next door was empty.

9.21.oldText: “I wish someone lived there,” Sara said. “It is so close that if there was a little girl in the attic, we could talk to each other through the windows and climb over to see each other, if we were not afraid of falling.”

9.22.oldText: The sky seemed so much closer than when one saw it from the street that Lottie was enchanted. From the attic window, among the chimney pots, the things happening in the world below seemed almost unreal. One scarcely believed in the existence of Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia and the schoolroom, and the rolling of wheels in the square seemed a sound from another world.

9.23.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” cried Lottie, cuddling into her protecting arm. “I like this attic — I like it! It is nicer than downstairs!”

9.24.oldText: “Look at that sparrow,” whispered Sara. “I wish I had some crumbs to throw to him.”

9.25.oldText: “I have some!” came in a little shriek from Lottie. “I have part of a bun in my pocket. I bought it with my penny yesterday, and I saved a bit.”

9.26.oldText: When they threw out a few crumbs, the sparrow jumped and flew away to a nearby chimney top. He was clearly not used to friends in attics, and unexpected crumbs startled him. But when Lottie stayed quite still and Sara chirped very softly — almost as if she were a sparrow herself — he saw that the thing that had alarmed him meant hospitality after all. He put his head on one side, and from his perch on the chimney looked down at the crumbs with twinkling eyes. Lottie could scarcely keep still.

9.27.oldText: “Will he come? Will he come?” she whispered.

9.28.oldText: “His eyes look as if he will,” Sara whispered back. “He is thinking and thinking whether he dares. Yes, he will! Yes, he is coming!”

9.29.oldText: He flew down and hopped towards the crumbs, but stopped a few inches away from them, putting his head on one side again, as if weighing the chances that Sara and Lottie might turn out to be big cats and pounce on him. At last his heart told him they were really nicer than they looked, and he hopped nearer and nearer, darted at the biggest crumb with a lightning peck, grabbed it, and carried it away to the other side of his chimney.

9.30.oldText: “Now he knows,” said Sara. “And he will come back for the others.”

9.31.oldText: He did come back, and even brought a friend, and the friend went away and brought a relative, and between them they made a hearty meal, twittering and chattering and exclaiming, stopping every now and then to put their heads on one side and examine Lottie and Sara. Lottie was so delighted that she quite forgot her first shocked impression of the attic. In fact, when she was lifted down from the table and returned to earthly things, as it were, Sara was able to point out many beauties in the room that she herself would not have suspected existed.

9.32.oldText: “It is so little and so high above everything,” she said, “that it is almost like a nest in a tree. The slanting ceiling is so funny. Look — you can scarcely stand up at this end of the room. And when morning begins to come, I can lie in bed and look right up into the sky through that flat window in the roof. It is like a square patch of light. If the sun is going to shine, little pink clouds float about, and I feel as if I could touch them. And if it rains, the drops patter and patter as if they were saying something nice. Then if there are stars, you can lie and try to count how many fit into the patch. It takes such a lot. And just look at that tiny, rusty grate in the corner. If it was polished and there was a fire in it, just think how nice it would be. You see, it's really a beautiful little room.”

9.33.oldText: She was walking round the small place, holding Lottie's hand and making gestures that described all the beauties she was making herself see. She quite made Lottie see them too. Lottie could always believe in the things Sara made pictures of.

9.34.oldText: “You see,” she said, “there could be a thick, soft blue Indian rug on the floor, and in that corner there could be a soft little sofa, with cushions to curl up on. And just over it there could be a shelf full of books, so that one could reach them easily. And there could be a fur rug before the fire, and hangings on the wall to cover up the whitewash, and pictures. They would have to be little ones, but they could be beautiful. And there could be a lamp with a deep rose-colored shade. And a table in the middle, with things to have tea with. And a little fat copper kettle singing on the hob. And the bed could be quite different. It could be made soft and covered with a lovely silk coverlet. It could be beautiful. And perhaps we could coax the sparrows until we made such friends with them that they would come and peck at the window and ask to be let in.”

9.35.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” cried Lottie. “I should like to live here!”

9.36.oldText: When Sara had persuaded her to go downstairs again, and, after setting her on her way, had come back to her attic, she stood in the middle of it and looked about her. The magic of her imaginings for Lottie had died away. The bed was hard and covered with its dingy quilt. The whitewashed wall showed its broken patches, the floor was cold and bare, the grate was broken and rusty, and the battered footstool, tilted sideways on its damaged leg, was the only seat in the room. She sat down on it for a few minutes and let her head drop into her hands. The mere fact that Lottie had come and gone again made things seem a little worse — just as perhaps prisoners feel a little more lonely after visitors come and go, leaving them behind.

9.37.oldText: “It's a lonely place,” she said. “Sometimes it's the loneliest place in the world.”

9.38.oldText: She was sitting like that when her attention was caught by a slight sound near her. She lifted her head to see where it came from, and if she had been a nervous child she would have leapt off the battered footstool in a great hurry. A large rat was sitting up on his hind legs and sniffing the air with an interested look. Some of Lottie's crumbs had dropped on the floor, and their scent had drawn him out of his hole.

9.39.oldText: He looked so odd and so like a gray-whiskered dwarf or gnome that Sara was rather fascinated. He looked at her with his bright eyes, as if he were asking a question. He was clearly so doubtful that one of the child's strange thoughts came into her mind.

9.40.oldText: “I dare say it is rather hard to be a rat,” she mused. “Nobody likes you. People jump and run away and scream out, ‘Oh, a horrid rat!' I shouldn't like people to scream and jump and say, ‘Oh, a horrid Sara!' the moment they saw me. And set traps for me, and pretend they were dinner. It's so different to be a sparrow. But nobody asked this rat if he wanted to be a rat when he was made. Nobody said, ‘Wouldn't you rather be a sparrow?'”

9.41.oldText: She had sat so quietly that the rat had begun to take courage. He was very much afraid of her, but perhaps he had a heart like the sparrow's, and it told him that she was not the sort of thing that pounced. He was very hungry. He had a wife and a large family in the wall, and they had had frightfully bad luck for several days. He had left the children crying bitterly, and he felt he would risk a good deal for a few crumbs, so he cautiously dropped onto his feet.

9.42.oldText: “Come on,” said Sara. “I'm not a trap. You can have them, poor thing! Prisoners in the Bastille used to make friends with rats. Suppose I make friends with you.”

9.43.oldText: How animals understand things I do not know, but it is certain that they do understand. Perhaps there is a language that is not made of words, and everything in the world understands it. Perhaps there is a soul hidden in everything, and it can always speak, without making a sound, to another soul. But whatever the reason, the rat knew from that moment that he was safe — even though he was a rat. He knew that this young human being sitting on the red footstool would not jump up and terrify him with wild, sharp noises, or throw heavy objects at him which, even if they did not crush him, would send him limping back to his hole. He was really a very nice rat, and meant no harm at all. When he had stood on his hind legs and sniffed the air, with his bright eyes fixed on Sara, he had hoped that she would understand this, and would not begin by hating him as an enemy. When the mysterious thing that speaks without words told him that she would not, he went softly toward the crumbs and began to eat them. As he ate, he glanced now and then at Sara, just as the sparrows had done, and his look was so apologetic that it touched her heart.

9.44.oldText: She sat and watched him without moving. One crumb was much larger than the others — in fact, it could scarcely be called a crumb. It was clear that he wanted that piece very much, but it lay quite near the footstool and he was still rather timid.

9.45.oldText: “I believe he wants it to carry to his family in the wall,” Sara thought. “If I do not stir at all, perhaps he will come and get it.”

9.46.oldText: She scarcely allowed herself to breathe, she was so deeply interested. The rat shuffled a little nearer and ate a few more crumbs, then he stopped and sniffed delicately, giving a side glance at the person on the footstool. Then he darted at the piece of bun with something very like the sudden boldness of the sparrow, and the instant he had it he fled back to the wall, slipped down a crack in the baseboard, and was gone.

9.47.oldText: “I knew he wanted it for his children,” said Sara. “I do believe I could make friends with him.”

9.48.oldText: A week or so later, on one of the rare nights when Ermengarde found it safe to sneak up to the attic, when she tapped on the door with the tips of her fingers, Sara did not come to her for two or three minutes. There was such a silence in the room at first that Ermengarde wondered if Sara could have fallen asleep. Then, to her surprise, she heard her give a little, low laugh and speak coaxingly to someone.

9.49.oldText: “There!” Ermengarde heard her say. “Take it and go home, Melchisedec! Go home to your wife!”

9.50.oldText: Almost at once Sara opened the door, and when she did, she found Ermengarde standing on the threshold with alarmed eyes.

9.51.oldText: “Who — who are you talking to, Sara?” she gasped out.

9.52.oldText: Sara drew her in cautiously, but she looked as if something pleased and amused her.

9.53.oldText: “You must promise not to be frightened — not to scream the least bit, or I can't tell you,” she answered.

9.54.oldText: Ermengarde felt almost ready to scream on the spot, but managed to control herself. She looked all round the attic and saw no one. And yet Sara had certainly been speaking to someone. She thought of ghosts.

9.55.oldText: “Is it — something that will frighten me?” she asked timidly.

9.56.oldText: “Some people are afraid of them,” said Sara. “I was at first — but I am not now.”

9.58.oldText: “No,” said Sara, laughing. “It was my rat.”

9.59.oldText: Ermengarde made one bound and landed in the middle of the little dingy bed. She tucked her feet under her nightgown and the red shawl. She did not scream, but she gasped with fright.

9.60.oldText: “Oh! Oh!” she cried under her breath. “A rat! A rat!”

9.61.oldText: “I was afraid you would be frightened,” said Sara. “But you needn't be. I am making him tame. He actually knows me and comes out when I call him. Are you too frightened to want to see him?”

9.62.oldText: The truth was that, as the days had gone on and, with the help of scraps brought up from the kitchen, her odd friendship had developed, she had gradually forgotten that the timid creature she was getting to know was just a rat.

9.63.oldText: At first Ermengarde was too alarmed to do anything but huddle in a heap on the bed and tuck up her feet, but the sight of Sara's calm little face and the story of Melchisedec's first appearance began at last to stir her curiosity, and she leaned forward over the edge of the bed and watched Sara go and kneel down by the hole in the baseboard.

9.64.oldText: “He — he won't run out quickly and jump on the bed, will he?” she said.

9.65.oldText: “No,” answered Sara. “He's as polite as we are. He is just like a person. Now watch!”

9.66.oldText: She began to make a low, whistling sound — so low and coaxing that it could only have been heard in complete stillness. She did it several times, looking entirely absorbed in it. Ermengarde thought she looked as if she were working a spell. And at last, clearly in answer, a gray-whiskered, bright-eyed head peeped out of the hole. Sara had some crumbs in her hand. She dropped them, and Melchisedec came quietly forth and ate them. A piece larger than the rest he took and carried in the most businesslike manner back to his home.

9.67.oldText: “You see,” said Sara, “that is for his wife and children. He is very nice. He only eats the little bits. After he goes back, I can always hear his family squeaking for joy. There are three kinds of squeaks. One kind is the children's, and one is Mrs. Melchisedec's, and one is Melchisedec's own.”

9.69.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” she said. “You are queer — but you are nice.”

9.70.oldText: “I know I am queer,” Sara admitted cheerfully, “and I try to be nice.” She rubbed her forehead with her little brown paw, and a puzzled, tender look came into her face. “Papa always laughed at me,” she said, “but I liked it. He thought I was queer, but he liked me to make up things. I — I can't help making up things. If I didn't, I don't believe I could live.” She paused and glanced around the attic. “I'm sure I couldn't live here,” she added in a low voice.

9.71.oldText: Ermengarde was interested, as she always was. “When you talk about things,” she said, “they seem as if they grew real. You talk about Melchisedec as if he was a person.”

9.72.oldText: “He is a person,” said Sara. “He gets hungry and frightened, just as we do. And he is married and has children. How do we know he doesn't think things, just as we do? His eyes look as if he was a person. That was why I gave him a name.”

9.73.oldText: She sat down on the floor in her favorite pose, holding her knees.

9.74.oldText: “Besides,” she said, “he is a Bastille rat sent to be my friend. I can always get a bit of bread the cook has thrown away, and it is quite enough to keep him alive.”

9.75.oldText: “Is it the Bastille still?” Ermengarde asked eagerly. “Do you always pretend it is the Bastille?”

9.76.oldText: “Nearly always,” answered Sara. “Sometimes I try to pretend it is another kind of place, but the Bastille is generally easiest — particularly when it is cold.”

9.77.oldText: Just at that moment Ermengarde almost jumped off the bed, she was so startled by a sound she heard. It was like two distinct knocks on the wall.

9.79.oldText: Sara got up from the floor and answered quite dramatically:

9.80.oldText: “It is the prisoner in the next cell.”

9.82.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara. “Listen — the two knocks meant, ‘Prisoner, are you there?'”

9.83.oldText: She knocked three times on the wall herself, as if in answer.

9.84.oldText: “That means, ‘Yes, I am here, and all is well.'”

9.85.oldText: Four knocks came from Becky's side of the wall.

9.86.oldText: “That means,” explained Sara, “‘Then, fellow-sufferer, we will sleep in peace. Good night.'”

9.88.oldText: “Oh, Sara!” she whispered joyfully. “It is like a story!”

9.89.oldText: “It is a story,” said Sara. “Everything's a story. You are a story — I am a story. Miss Minchin is a story.”

9.90.oldText: And she sat down again and talked until Ermengarde forgot that she was a sort of escaped prisoner herself, and had to be reminded by Sara that she could not stay in the Bastille all night, but must steal noiselessly downstairs again and creep back into her deserted bed.

10.0.oldText: But it was risky for Ermengarde and Lottie to make pilgrimages up to the attic. They could never be quite sure when Sara would be there, and they could rarely be certain that Miss Amelia would not make an inspection round of the bedrooms after the pupils were supposed to be asleep. So their visits were rare, and Sara lived a strange and lonely life. It was lonelier downstairs than up in her attic. She had no one to talk to. When she was sent out on errands and walked through the streets — a forlorn little figure carrying a basket or a parcel, trying to hold her hat on when the wind blew, and feeling water soak through her shoes when it rained — she felt as if the crowds hurrying past made her loneliness greater. When she had been Princess Sara, driving through the streets in her carriage, or walking with Mariette beside her, the sight of her bright, eager little face and pretty coats and hats had often made people look after her. A happy, beautifully cared-for little girl naturally attracts attention. Shabby, poorly dressed children are not rare enough or pretty enough to make people turn around and smile. No one looked at Sara these days, and no one seemed to see her as she hurried along the crowded pavements. She had begun to grow very fast, and since she was dressed only in whatever plain remnants of her old wardrobe still fit, she knew she looked very strange indeed. All her valuable clothes had been disposed of, and she was expected to wear the leftovers as long as she could squeeze into them. Sometimes, when she passed a shop window with a mirror in it, she almost laughed out loud at the glimpse of herself, and sometimes her face went red and she bit her lip and turned away.

10.1.oldText: In the evening, when she passed houses with lighted windows, she liked to look into the warm rooms and amuse herself by imagining things about the people sitting before the fires or around the tables. It always interested her to catch glimpses of rooms before the shutters were closed. There were several families in the square where Miss Minchin lived that she had become quite familiar with in her own way. The one she liked best she called the Large Family. She called them the Large Family not because the members were big — most of them were little — but because there were so many of them. There were eight children in the Large Family, and a stout, rosy mother, and a stout, rosy father, and a stout, rosy grandmother, and any number of servants. The eight children were always either being taken out for a walk or pushed in prams by comfortable nurses, or going for a drive with their mamma, or flying to the door in the evening to meet their papa and kiss him and dance around him and pull off his overcoat to look in the pockets for packages, or crowding at the nursery windows and looking out and pushing each other and laughing. In fact, they were always doing something enjoyable that suited the tastes of a large family. Sara was very fond of them, and had given them names out of books — quite romantic names. She called them the Montmorencys when she did not call them the Large Family. The fat, fair baby with the lace cap was Ethelberta Beauchamp Montmorency; the next baby was Violet Cholmondeley Montmorency; the little boy who could just stagger and who had such round legs was Sydney Cecil Vivian Montmorency; and then came Lilian Evangeline Maud Marion, Rosalind Gladys, Guy Clarence, Veronica Eustacia, and Claude Harold Hector.

10.2.oldText: One evening a very funny thing happened — though, perhaps, in one sense it was not a funny thing at all.

10.3.oldText: Several of the Montmorencys were clearly going to a children's party, and just as Sara was about to pass their door they were crossing the pavement to get into the carriage waiting for them. Veronica Eustacia and Rosalind Gladys, in white-lace dresses and lovely sashes, had just got in, and Guy Clarence, aged five, was following them. He was such a pretty little fellow, with rosy cheeks and blue eyes and a darling little round head covered in curls, that Sara forgot her basket and shabby cloak entirely. In fact, she forgot everything except that she wanted to look at him for a moment. So she paused and looked.

10.4.oldText: It was Christmas time, and the Large Family had been hearing many stories about poor children with no mammas or papas to fill their stockings or take them to the pantomime — children who were cold and thinly dressed and hungry. In the stories, kind people — sometimes little boys and girls with tender hearts — always saw the poor children and gave them money or rich gifts, or took them home to beautiful dinners. Guy Clarence had been moved to tears that very afternoon by such a story, and he had been burning with a desire to find such a poor child and give her a certain sixpence he owned, and so provide for her for life. A whole sixpence, he was sure, would mean riches forever. As he crossed the strip of red carpet laid across the pavement from the door to the carriage, he had this very sixpence in the pocket of his very short sailor trousers. And just as Rosalind Gladys got into the carriage and bounced on the seat to feel the cushions spring under her, he saw Sara standing on the wet pavement in her shabby dress and hat, with her old basket on her arm, looking at him hungrily.

10.5.oldText: He thought her eyes looked hungry because perhaps she had had nothing to eat for a long time. He did not know that they looked that way because she was hungry for the warm, merry life his home held and his rosy face spoke of, and that she had a hungry wish to snatch him in her arms and kiss him. He only knew that she had big eyes and a thin face and thin legs and a shabby basket and poor clothes. So he put his hand in his pocket and found his sixpence and walked up to her kindly.

10.6.oldText: “Here, poor little girl,” he said. “Here is a sixpence. I will give it to you.”

10.7.oldText: Sara started, and suddenly realised that she looked exactly like the poor children she had seen, in her better days, waiting on the pavement to watch her step out of her carriage. And she had often given them pennies. Her face went red and then it went pale, and for a second she felt as if she could not take the dear little sixpence.

10.8.oldText: “Oh, no!” she said. “Oh, no, thank you; I really mustn't take it!”

10.9.oldText: Her voice was so unlike an ordinary street child's voice, and her manner was so like that of a well-bred little person, that Veronica Eustacia (whose real name was Janet) and Rosalind Gladys (who was really called Nora) leaned forward to listen.

10.10.oldText: But Guy Clarence was not going to be stopped in his kindness. He pushed the sixpence into her hand.

10.11.oldText: “Yes, you must take it, poor little girl!” he insisted firmly. “You can buy things to eat with it. It is a whole sixpence!”

10.12.oldText: There was something so honest and kind in his face, and he looked so likely to be heartbroken if she refused, that Sara knew she must not say no. To be that proud would be a cruel thing. So she actually put her pride in her pocket, though it must be admitted that her cheeks burned.

10.13.oldText: “Thank you,” she said. “You are a kind, kind little darling thing.” And as he scrambled joyfully into the carriage, she walked away, trying to smile, though she caught her breath quickly and her eyes were shining through a mist. She had known that she looked odd and shabby, but until now she had not known she might be taken for a beggar.

10.14.oldText: As the Large Family's carriage drove away, the children inside were talking with excited interest.

10.15.oldText: “Oh, Donald,” (this was Guy Clarence's name), Janet exclaimed, alarmed, “why did you offer that little girl your sixpence? I'm sure she is not a beggar!”

10.16.oldText: “She didn't speak like a beggar!” cried Nora. “And her face didn't really look like a beggar's face!”

10.17.oldText: “Besides, she didn't beg,” said Janet. “I was so afraid she might be angry with you. You know, it makes people angry to be taken for beggars when they are not beggars.”

10.18.oldText: “She wasn't angry,” said Donald, a little bit dismayed but still firm. “She laughed a little, and she said I was a kind, kind little darling thing. And I was!” — stoutly. “It was my whole sixpence.”

10.20.oldText: “A beggar girl would never have said that,” Janet decided. “She would have said, ‘Thank yer kindly, little gentleman — thank yer, sir;’ and perhaps she would have bobbed a curtsy.”

10.21.oldText: Sara knew nothing about it, but from that time on the Large Family was as deeply interested in her as she was in them. Faces would appear at the nursery windows when she passed, and many discussions about her were held around the fire.

10.22.oldText: “She is some kind of servant at the seminary,” Janet said. “I don't believe she belongs to anybody. I think she is an orphan. But she is not a beggar, however shabby she looks.”

10.23.oldText: And after that, they all called her “The-little-girl-who-is-not-a-beggar,” which was, of course, rather a long name, and sounded very funny sometimes when the youngest ones said it in a hurry.

10.24.oldText: Sara managed to bore a hole in the sixpence and hung it on an old bit of narrow ribbon round her neck. Her affection for the Large Family grew — as, indeed, her affection for everything she could love grew. She grew fonder and fonder of Becky, and she used to look forward to the two mornings a week when she went into the schoolroom to give the little ones their French lesson. Her small pupils loved her, and competed with each other for the privilege of standing close to her and slipping their small hands into hers. It fed her hungry heart to feel them nestling up to her. She had made such friends with the sparrows that when she stood on the table, put her head and shoulders out of the attic window, and chirped, she heard almost at once a flutter of wings and answering twitters, and a little flock of dingy town birds appeared and landed on the slates to talk to her and make a fuss over the crumbs she scattered. With Melchisedec she had become so close that he actually brought Mrs. Melchisedec with him sometimes, and now and then one or two of his children. She used to talk to him, and somehow he looked quite as if he understood.

10.25.oldText: A rather strange feeling had grown in her mind about Emily, who always sat and looked on at everything. It came to her in one of her moments of great desolation. She would have liked to believe, or pretend to believe, that Emily understood and felt sorry for her. She did not like to admit to herself that her only companion could feel and hear nothing. She used to put her in a chair sometimes and sit opposite to her on the old red footstool, and stare and pretend about her until her own eyes would grow large with something that was almost like fear — particularly at night, when everything was so still, and the only sound in the attic was the occasional sudden scurry and squeak of Melchisedec's family in the wall. One of her “pretends” was that Emily was a kind of good witch who could protect her. Sometimes, after staring at her until she was worked up to the highest pitch of fancy, she would ask her questions and find herself ALMOST feeling as if she would presently answer. But she never did.

10.26.oldText: “As to answering, though,” said Sara, trying to console herself, “I don't answer very often. I never answer when I can help it. When people are insulting you, there is nothing as good as not saying a word — just to look at them and THINK. Miss Minchin turns pale with rage when I do it, Miss Amelia looks frightened, and so do the girls. When you will not lose your temper, people know you are stronger than they are, because you are strong enough to hold in your rage, and they are not, and they say stupid things they wish afterwards they hadn't said. There is nothing as strong as rage, except what makes you hold it in — that's stronger. It's a good thing not to answer your enemies. I scarcely ever do. Perhaps Emily is more like me than I am like myself. Perhaps she would rather not answer her friends, even. She keeps it all in her heart.”

10.27.oldText: But although she tried to satisfy herself with these arguments, she did not find it easy.
