When, after a long, hard day in which she had been sent here and there, sometimes on long errands through wind and cold and rain, she came in wet and hungry, only to be sent out again because nobody chose to remember she was only a child whose slim legs might be tired and whose small body might be chilled; when she had been given only harsh words and cold, slighting looks for thanks; when the cook had been vulgar and rude; when Miss Minchin had been in her worst mood, and when she had seen the girls sneering at her shabbiness — then she was not always able to comfort her sore, proud, desolate heart with fancies, while Emily merely sat upright in her old chair and stared.

10.28.oldText: One of these nights, when she came up to the attic cold and hungry, with a tempest raging in her young breast, Emily's stare seemed so vacant, her sawdust legs and arms so blank, that Sara lost all control over herself. There was nobody but Emily — no one in the world. And there she sat.

10.29.oldText: “I shall die soon,” she said at first.

10.31.oldText: “I can't bear this,” said the poor child, trembling. “I know I shall die. I'm cold; I'm wet; I'm starving to death. I've walked a thousand miles today, and they have done nothing but scold me from morning until night. And because I could not find that last thing the cook sent me for, they would not give me any supper. Some men laughed at me because my old shoes made me slip down in the mud. I'm covered with mud now. And they laughed. Do you hear?”

10.32.oldText: She looked at the staring glass eyes and complacent face, and suddenly a kind of heartbroken rage seized her. She lifted her little furious hand and knocked Emily off the chair, bursting into a passion of sobbing — Sara, who never cried.

10.33.oldText: “You are nothing but a DOLL!” she cried. “Nothing but a doll — doll — doll! You care for nothing. You are stuffed with sawdust. You never had a heart. Nothing could ever make you feel. You are a DOLL!” Emily lay on the floor, with her legs ignominiously doubled up over her head, and a new flat place on the end of her nose; but she was calm, even dignified. Sara hid her face in her arms. The rats in the wall began to fight and bite each other and squeak and scramble. Melchisedec was punishing some of his family.

10.34.oldText: Sara's sobs gradually quieted. It was so unlike her to break down that she was surprised at herself. After a while she raised her face and looked at Emily, who seemed to be gazing at her round the side of one angle, and somehow, by this time, actually with a kind of glassy-eyed sympathy. Sara bent and picked her up. Remorse caught up with her. She even smiled at herself a very little smile.

10.35.oldText: “You can't help being a doll,” she said with a resigned sigh, “any more than Lavinia and Jessie can help having no sense. We are not all made alike. Perhaps you do your sawdust best.” And she kissed her and shook her clothes straight, and put her back on her chair.

10.36.oldText: She had wished very much that someone would take the empty house next door. She wished it because of the attic window, which was so close to hers. It seemed as if it would be so nice to see it propped open one day and a head and shoulders rising out of the square opening.

10.37.oldText: “If it looked a nice head,” she thought, “I might begin by saying, ‘Good morning,’ and all sorts of things might happen. But, of course, it's not really likely that anyone but under-servants would sleep there.”

10.38.oldText: One morning, on turning the corner of the square after a visit to the grocer's, the butcher's, and the baker's, she saw, to her great delight, that during her rather long absence, a van full of furniture had stopped before the next house. The front doors were thrown open, and men in shirt sleeves were going in and out carrying heavy packages and pieces of furniture.

10.39.oldText: “It's taken!” she said. “It really IS taken! Oh, I do hope a nice head will look out of the attic window!”

10.40.oldText: She would almost have liked to join the group of loiterers who had stopped on the pavement to watch the things being carried in. She had an idea that if she could see some of the furniture, she could guess something about the people it belonged to.

10.41.oldText: “Miss Minchin's tables and chairs are just like her,” she thought. “I remember thinking that the first minute I saw her, even though I was so little. I told papa afterwards, and he laughed and said it was true. I am sure the Large Family have fat, comfortable armchairs and sofas, and I can see that their red-flowery wallpaper is exactly like them. It's warm and cheerful and kind-looking and happy.”

10.42.oldText: She was sent out for parsley to the greengrocer's later in the day, and when she came up the area steps her heart gave quite a quick beat of recognition. Several pieces of furniture had been set out of the van onto the pavement. There was a beautiful table of elaborately carved teakwood, and some chairs, and a screen covered with rich Oriental embroidery. The sight of them gave her a strange, homesick feeling. She had seen things very like them in India. One of the things Miss Minchin had taken from her was a carved teakwood desk her father had sent her.

10.43.oldText: “They are beautiful things,” she said. “They look as if they ought to belong to a nice person. All the things look rather grand. I suppose it is a rich family.”

10.44.oldText: The vans of furniture came and were unloaded and gave place to others all day. Several times Sara happened to have a chance of seeing things being carried in. It became plain that she had been right in guessing the newcomers were people of large means. All the furniture was rich and beautiful, and a great deal of it was Oriental. Wonderful rugs and draperies and ornaments were taken from the vans, many pictures, and books enough for a library. Among other things there was a magnificent god Buddha in a splendid shrine.

10.45.oldText: “Someone in the family MUST have been in India,” Sara thought. “They have got used to Indian things and like them. I AM glad. I shall feel as if they were friends, even if a head never looks out of the attic window.”

10.46.oldText: When she was taking in the evening's milk for the cook (there was really no odd job she was not called on to do), she saw something happen that made the situation more interesting than ever. The handsome, rosy man who was the father of the Large Family walked across the square in the most matter-of-fact manner, and ran up the steps of the next-door house. He ran up them as if he felt quite at home and expected to run up and down them many a time in the future. He stayed inside quite a long time, and several times came out and gave directions to the workmen, as if he had a right to do so. It was quite certain that he was in some close way connected with the newcomers and was acting for them.

10.47.oldText: “If the new people have children,” Sara guessed, “the Large Family children will be sure to come and play with them, and they MIGHT come up into the attic just for fun.”

10.48.oldText: At night, after her work was done, Becky came in to see her fellow prisoner and bring her news.

10.49.oldText: “It's a' Nindian gentleman that's comin' to live next door, miss,” she said. “I don't know whether he's a black gentleman or not, but he's a Nindian one. He's very rich, an' he's ill, an' the gentleman of the Large Family is his lawyer. He's had a lot of trouble, an' it's made him ill an' low in his mind. He worships idols, miss. He's an 'eathen an' bows down to wood an' stone. I seen a' idol bein' carried in for him to worship. Somebody had oughter send him a trac'. You can get a trac' for a penny.”

10.51.oldText: “I don't believe he worships that idol,” she said. “Some people like to keep them to look at because they are interesting. My papa had a beautiful one, and he did not worship it.”

10.52.oldText: But Becky was rather inclined to prefer to believe that the new neighbour was “an 'eathen.” It sounded so much more romantic than that he should merely be the ordinary kind of gentleman who went to church with a prayer book. She sat and talked long that night about what he would be like, what his wife would be like if he had one, and what his children would be like if they had children. Sara saw that privately Becky could not help hoping very much that they would all be black, and would wear turbans, and, above all, that — like their parent — they would all be “'eathens.”

10.53.oldText: “I never lived next door to no 'eathens, miss,” she said. “I should like to see what sort o' ways they'd have.”

10.54.oldText: It was several weeks before her curiosity was satisfied, and then it was revealed that the new occupant had neither wife nor children. He was a solitary man with no family at all, and it was clear that he was shattered in health and unhappy in mind.

10.55.oldText: A carriage drove up one day and stopped before the house. When the footman climbed down from the box and opened the door, the gentleman who was the father of the Large Family got out first. After him, a nurse in uniform stepped down, and then two manservants came down the steps. They came to help their master, who, when he was helped out of the carriage, turned out to be a man with a haggard, distressed face, and a skeleton body wrapped in furs. He was carried up the steps, and the head of the Large Family went with him, looking very anxious. Shortly afterwards a doctor's carriage arrived, and the doctor went in — plainly to take care of him.

10.56.oldText: “There is such a yellow gentleman next door, Sara,” Lottie whispered at the French class afterwards. “Do you think he is a Chinee? The geography says the Chinee men are yellow.”

10.57.oldText: “No, he is not Chinese,” Sara whispered back. “He is very ill. Go on with your exercise, Lottie. ‘Non, monsieur. Je n'ai pas le canif de mon oncle.’”

10.58.oldText: That was the beginning of the story of the Indian gentleman.

11.0.oldText: There were fine sunsets even in the square, sometimes. One could only see parts of them, however, between the chimneys and over the roofs. From the kitchen windows one could not see them at all, and could only guess that they were going on because the bricks looked warm and the air rosy or yellow for a while, or perhaps one saw a blazing glow strike a particular pane of glass somewhere. There was, however, one place from which one could see all their splendour: the piles of red or gold clouds in the west; the purple ones edged with dazzling brightness; the little fleecy, floating ones, tinged with rose-colour and looking like flights of pink doves scurrying across the blue in a great hurry if there was a wind. The place where one could see all this, and seem at the same time to breathe a purer air, was, of course, the attic window. When the square suddenly seemed to begin to glow in an enchanted way and look wonderful in spite of its sooty trees and railings, Sara knew something was going on in the sky. Whenever it was at all possible to leave the kitchen without being missed or called back, she invariably stole away and crept up the flights of stairs, and, climbing on the old table, got her head and body as far out of the window as possible. When she had managed this, she always drew a long breath and looked all around her. It used to seem as if she had all the sky and the world to herself. No one else ever looked out of the other attics. Generally the skylights were closed; but even if they were propped open to let in air, no one ever seemed to come near them. And there Sara would stand, sometimes turning her face up to the blue, which seemed so friendly and near — just like a lovely vaulted ceiling — sometimes watching the west and all the wonderful things that happened there: the clouds melting or drifting or waiting softly to be changed pink or crimson or snow-white or purple or pale dove-grey. Sometimes they made islands or great mountains enclosing lakes of deep turquoise-blue, or liquid amber, or chrysoprase-green; sometimes dark headlands jutted out into strange, lost seas; sometimes slender strips of wonderful lands joined other wonderful lands together. There were places where it seemed that one could run or climb or stand and wait to see what would come next — until, perhaps, as it all melted, one could float away. At least it seemed so to Sara, and nothing had ever been quite so beautiful to her as the things she saw as she stood on the table, her body half out of the skylight, the sparrows twittering with sunset softness on the slates. The sparrows always seemed to her to twitter with a kind of subdued softness just when these marvels were going on.

11.1.oldText: There was such a sunset as this a few days after the Indian gentleman was brought to his new home; and, as it happened, the afternoon's work was done in the kitchen and nobody had ordered her to go anywhere or do any task. Sara found it easier than usual to slip away and go upstairs.

11.2.oldText: She climbed onto her table and stood looking out. It was a wonderful moment. There were floods of molten gold covering the west, as if a glorious tide was sweeping over the world. A deep, rich yellow light filled the air; the birds flying across the tops of the houses showed quite black against it.

11.3.oldText: “It's a Splendid one,” Sara said softly to herself. “It makes me feel almost afraid — as if something strange was just about to happen. The Splendid ones always make me feel like that.”

11.4.oldText: She suddenly turned her head because she heard a sound a few yards away from her. It was an odd sound, like a queer little squeaky chattering. It came from the window of the next attic. Someone had come to look at the sunset, just as she had. There was a head and part of a body emerging from the skylight, but it was not the head or body of a little girl or a housemaid. It was the picturesque white-swathed form and dark-faced, gleaming-eyed, white-turbaned head of a native Indian manservant — “a Lascar,” Sara said to herself quickly — and the sound she had heard came from a small monkey he held in his arms as if he were fond of it, which was snuggling and chattering against his chest.

11.5.oldText: As Sara looked toward him, he looked toward her. The first thing she thought was that his dark face looked sorrowful and homesick. She felt absolutely sure he had come up to look at the sun, because he had seen it so seldom in England that he longed for a sight of it. She looked at him with interest for a second, and then smiled across the slates. She had learned how comforting a smile, even from a stranger, can be.

11.6.oldText: Hers was clearly a pleasure to him. His whole expression changed, and he showed such gleaming white teeth as he smiled back that it was as if a light had been lit in his dusky face. The friendly look in Sara's eyes was always very effective when people felt tired or dull.

11.7.oldText: It was perhaps in giving her his salute that he loosened his hold on the monkey. The monkey was an impish creature and always ready for adventure, and probably the sight of a little girl excited him. He suddenly broke loose, jumped onto the slates, ran across them chattering, and actually leaped onto Sara's shoulder, and from there down into her attic room. It made her laugh and delighted her; but she knew he must be returned to his master — if the Lascar was his master — and she wondered how this was to be done. Would he let her catch him, or would he be naughty and refuse to be caught, and perhaps get away and run off over the roofs and be lost? That would not do at all. Perhaps he belonged to the Indian gentleman, and the poor man was fond of him.

11.8.oldText: She turned to the Lascar, glad that she still remembered some of the Hindustani she had learned when she lived with her father. She could make the man understand. She spoke to him in the language he knew.

11.9.oldText: “Will he let me catch him?” she asked.

11.10.oldText: She thought she had never seen more surprise and delight than the dark face expressed when she spoke in the familiar tongue. The truth was that the poor fellow felt as if his gods had stepped in, and the kind little voice came from heaven itself. At once Sara saw that he had been used to European children. He poured out a flood of respectful thanks. He was the servant of Missee Sahib. The monkey was a good monkey and would not bite; but, unfortunately, he was difficult to catch. He would flee from one spot to another, like lightning. He was disobedient, though not evil. Ram Dass knew him as if he were his child, and Ram Dass he would sometimes obey, but not always. If Missee Sahib would permit Ram Dass, he himself could cross the roof to her room, enter through the window, and recover the unworthy little animal. But he was clearly afraid Sara might think he was taking a great liberty and perhaps would not let him come.

11.11.oldText: But Sara gave him leave at once.

11.14.oldText: “Then come,” she said; “he is flying from side to side of the room as if he was frightened.”

11.15.oldText: Ram Dass slipped through his attic window and crossed to hers as steadily and lightly as if he had walked on roofs all his life. He slipped through the skylight and dropped onto his feet without a sound. Then he turned to Sara and bowed again. The monkey saw him and uttered a little scream. Ram Dass quickly took the precaution of shutting the skylight, and then went after him. It was not a very long chase. The monkey kept it going for a few minutes, evidently for the sheer fun of it, but soon he sprang chattering onto Ram Dass's shoulder and sat there chattering and clinging to his neck with a weird little skinny arm.

11.16.oldText: Ram Dass thanked Sara deeply. She had seen that his quick native eyes had taken in at a glance all the bare shabbiness of the room, but he spoke to her as if he were speaking to the little daughter of a rajah, and pretended he noticed nothing. He did not presume to stay more than a few moments after he had caught the monkey, and those moments were given to further deep and grateful bows in return for her kindness. This little evil one, he said, stroking the monkey, was, in truth, not so evil as he seemed, and his master, who was ill, was sometimes amused by him. He would have been made sad if his favourite had run away and been lost. Then he salaamed once more and got back through the skylight and across the slates with as much agility as the monkey himself had shown.

11.17.oldText: When he had gone, Sara stood in the middle of her attic and thought of many things his face and manner had brought back to her. The sight of his native costume and the deep reverence in his manner stirred all her past memories. It seemed strange to remember that she — the drudge whom the cook had insulted only an hour ago — had only a few years ago been surrounded by people who all treated her as Ram Dass had treated her; who salaamed when she went by, whose foreheads almost touched the ground when she spoke to them, who were her servants and her slaves. It was like a sort of dream. It was all over, and it could never come back. It certainly seemed that there was no way any change could happen. She knew what Miss Minchin intended for her future. As long as she was too young to be used as a regular teacher, she would be used as an errand girl and servant, and yet expected to remember what she had learned and somehow learn more. Most of her evenings she was supposed to spend at study, and at various irregular intervals she was examined and knew she would be sharply scolded if she had not advanced as expected. The truth, in fact, was that Miss Minchin knew Sara was too eager to learn to need teachers. Give her books, and she would devour them and end by knowing them by heart. She could be trusted to be ready to teach a good deal in a few years' time. This was what would happen: when she was older she would be expected to drudge in the schoolroom as she drudged now in various parts of the house; they would have to give her more respectable clothes, but they were sure to be plain and ugly and to make her look somehow like a servant. That was all there seemed to be to look forward to, and Sara stood quite still for several minutes thinking it over.

11.18.oldText: Then a thought came back to her which made the colour rise in her cheek and a spark light itself in her eyes. She straightened her thin little body and lifted her head.

11.19.oldText: “Whatever comes,” she said, “cannot alter one thing. If I am a princess in rags and tatters, I can be a princess inside. It would be easy to be a princess if I were dressed in cloth of gold, but it is a great deal more of a triumph to be one all the time when no one knows it. There was Marie Antoinette when she was in prison and her throne was gone and she had only a black gown on, and her hair was white, and they insulted her and called her Widow Capet. She was a great deal more like a queen then than when she was so gay and everything was so grand. I like her best then. Those howling mobs of people did not frighten her. She was stronger than they were, even when they cut her head off.”

11.20.oldText: This was not a new thought, but quite an old one by now. It had consoled her through many a bitter day, and she had gone about the house with an expression on her face that Miss Minchin could not understand and that was a source of great annoyance to her, as it seemed as if the child were mentally living a life that held her above the rest of the world. It was as if she scarcely heard the rude and bitter things said to her; or, if she heard them, did not care for them at all. Sometimes, in the middle of some harsh, bullying speech, Miss Minchin would find the still, unchildish eyes fixed on her with something like a proud smile in them. At such times she did not know that Sara was saying to herself:

11.21.oldText: “You don't know that you are saying these things to a princess, and that if I chose I could wave my hand and order you to execution. I only spare you because I am a princess, and you are a poor, stupid, unkind, vulgar old thing, and don't know any better.”

11.22.oldText: This used to interest and amuse her more than anything else; and queer and fanciful as it was, she found comfort in it and it was a good thing for her. While the thought held her, she could not be made rude and spiteful by the rudeness and spite of those around her.

11.23.oldText: “A princess must be polite,” she said to herself.

11.24.oldText: And so when the servants, taking their tone from their mistress, were rude and ordered her about, she would hold her head high and reply to them with a quaint courtesy that often made them stare at her.

11.25.oldText: “She's got more airs and graces than if she come from Buckingham Palace, that young one,” said the cook, chuckling a little sometimes. “I lose my temper with her often enough, but I will say she never forgets her manners. ‘If you please, cook’; ‘Will you be so kind, cook?’ ‘I beg your pardon, cook’; ‘May I trouble you, cook?’ She drops 'em about the kitchen as if they was nothing.”

11.26.oldText: The morning after meeting Ram Dass and his monkey, Sara was in the schoolroom with her small pupils. Having finished giving them their lessons, she was putting the French exercise-books together and thinking, as she did so, of the various things royal people in disguise were called upon to do: Alfred the Great, for instance, burning the cakes and getting his ears boxed by the wife of the cowherd. How frightened she must have been when she found out what she had done. If Miss Minchin should find out that she — Sara, whose toes were almost sticking out of her boots — was a princess — a real one! The look in her eyes was exactly the look Miss Minchin most disliked. She would not have it; she was quite near her and was so enraged that she actually flew at her and boxed her ears — exactly as the cowherd's wife had boxed King Alfred's. It made Sara start. She woke from her dream at the shock, and, catching her breath, stood still for a second. Then, not knowing she was going to do it, she broke into a little laugh.

11.27.oldText: “What are you laughing at, you bold, impudent child?” Miss Minchin exclaimed.

11.28.oldText: It took Sara a few seconds to control herself enough to remember that she was a princess. Her cheeks were red and stinging from the blows she had received.

11.30.oldText: “Beg my pardon immediately,” said Miss Minchin.

11.31.oldText: Sara hesitated a second before she replied.

11.32.oldText: “I will beg your pardon for laughing, if it was rude,” she then said; “but I won't beg your pardon for thinking.”

11.33.oldText: “What were you thinking?” demanded Miss Minchin. “How dare you think? What were you thinking?”

11.34.oldText: Jessie tittered, and she and Lavinia nudged each other in unison. All the girls looked up from their books to listen. Really, it always interested them a little when Miss Minchin attacked Sara. Sara always said something queer, and never seemed the least bit frightened. She was not in the least frightened now, though her boxed ears were scarlet and her eyes were as bright as stars.

11.35.oldText: “I was thinking,” she answered grandly and politely, “that you did not know what you were doing.”

11.36.oldText: “That I did not know what I was doing?” Miss Minchin almost gasped.

11.37.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara, “and I was thinking what would happen if I were a princess and you boxed my ears — what I should do to you. And I was thinking that if I were one, you would never dare to do it, whatever I said or did. And I was thinking how surprised and frightened you would be if you suddenly found out —”

11.38.oldText: She had the imagined future so clearly before her eyes that she spoke in a way that had an effect even on Miss Minchin. It almost seemed for the moment to her narrow, unimaginative mind that there must be some real power hidden behind this candid daring.

11.40.oldText: “That I really was a princess,” said Sara, “and could do anything — anything I liked.”

11.41.oldText: Every pair of eyes in the room widened to its full limit. Lavinia leaned forward on her seat to look.

11.42.oldText: “Go to your room,” cried Miss Minchin, breathless, “this instant! Leave the schoolroom! Attend to your lessons, young ladies!”

11.44.oldText: “Excuse me for laughing if it was impolite,” she said, and walked out of the room, leaving Miss Minchin struggling with her rage, and the girls whispering over their books.

11.45.oldText: “Did you see her? Did you see how queer she looked?” Jessie burst out. “I shouldn't be at all surprised if she did turn out to be something. Suppose she should!”

12.0.oldText: When you live in a row of houses, it is interesting to think about the things being done and said on the other side of the wall of the very rooms you are living in. Sara was fond of amusing herself by trying to imagine the things hidden by the wall that divided the Select Seminary from the Indian gentleman's house. She knew that the schoolroom was next to the Indian gentleman's study, and she hoped that the wall was thick so that the noise made sometimes after lesson hours would not disturb him.

12.1.oldText: “I am growing quite fond of him,” she said to Ermengarde. “I should not like him to be disturbed. I have adopted him as a friend. You can do that with people you never speak to at all. You can just watch them, and think about them and feel sorry for them, until they seem almost like relations. I'm quite worried sometimes when I see the doctor call twice a day.”

12.2.oldText: “I have very few relations,” said Ermengarde, thoughtfully, “and I'm very glad of it. I don't like the ones I have. My two aunts are always saying, ‘Dear me, Ermengarde! You are very fat. You shouldn't eat sweets,’ and my uncle is always asking me things like, ‘When did Edward the Third come to the throne?’ and, ‘Who died of a surfeit of lampreys?’”

12.4.oldText: “People you never speak to can't ask you questions like that,” she said. “And I'm sure the Indian gentleman wouldn't, even if he was quite close with you. I am fond of him.”

12.5.oldText: She had become fond of the Large Family because they looked happy; but she had become fond of the Indian gentleman because he looked unhappy. He had clearly not fully recovered from some very serious illness. In the kitchen — where, of course, the servants somehow knew everything — there was much discussion of his case. He was not really an Indian gentleman, but an Englishman who had lived in India. He had met with great misfortunes that had at one point so endangered his whole fortune that he had thought himself ruined and disgraced forever. The shock had been so great that he had almost died of brain fever; and ever since he had been shattered in health, though his fortunes had changed and all his possessions had been restored to him. His trouble and danger had been connected with mines.

12.6.oldText: “And mines with diamonds in 'em!” said the cook. “No savin's of mine never goes into no mines — particular diamond ones” — with a side glance at Sara. “We all know somethin' of THEM.”

12.7.oldText: “He felt as my papa felt,” Sara thought. “He was ill as my papa was; but he did not die.”

12.8.oldText: So her heart was drawn to him more than before. When she was sent out at night, she sometimes felt quite glad, because there was always a chance that the curtains of the house next door might not yet be closed and she could look into the warm room and see her adopted friend. When no one was about she sometimes used to stop, and, holding to the iron railings, wish him good night as if he could hear her.

12.9.oldText: “Perhaps you can FEEL if you can't hear,” was her fancy. “Perhaps kind thoughts reach people somehow, even through windows and doors and walls. Perhaps you feel a little warm and comforted, and don't know why, when I am standing here in the cold and hoping you will get well and happy again. I am so sorry for you,” she would whisper in an intense little voice. “I wish you had a ‘Little Missus’ who could pet you as I used to pet papa when he had a headache. I should like to be your ‘Little Missus’ myself, poor dear! Good night — good night. God bless you!”

12.10.oldText: She would go away, feeling quite comforted and a little warmer herself. Her sympathy was so strong that it seemed as if it MUST reach him somehow as he sat alone in his armchair by the fire, nearly always in a great dressing gown, and nearly always with his forehead resting in his hand as he gazed hopelessly into the fire. He looked to Sara like a man who had a trouble on his mind still, not merely like one whose troubles were all in the past.

12.11.oldText: “He always seems as if he were thinking of something that hurts him NOW,” she said to herself, “but he has got his money back and he will get over his brain fever in time, so he ought not to look like that. I wonder if there is something else.”

12.12.oldText: If there was something else — something even servants did not hear of — she could not help believing that the father of the Large Family knew it — the gentleman she called Mr. Montmorency. Mr. Montmorency went to see him often, and Mrs. Montmorency and all the little Montmorencys went too, though less often. He seemed particularly fond of the two elder little girls — the Janet and Nora who had been so alarmed when their small brother Donald had given Sara his sixpence. He had, in fact, a very tender place in his heart for all children, and particularly for little girls. Janet and Nora were as fond of him as he was of them, and looked forward with the greatest pleasure to the afternoons when they were allowed to cross the square and pay their well-behaved little visits to him. They were extremely proper little visits because he was an invalid.

12.13.oldText: “He is a poor thing,” said Janet, “and he says we cheer him up. We try to cheer him up very quietly.”

12.14.oldText: Janet was the head of the family, and kept the rest of them in order. It was she who decided when it was wise to ask the Indian gentleman to tell stories about India, and it was she who saw when he was tired and it was time to steal quietly away and tell Ram Dass to go to him. They were very fond of Ram Dass. He could have told any number of stories if he had been able to speak anything but Hindustani. The Indian gentleman's real name was Mr. Carrisford, and Janet told Mr. Carrisford about meeting the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar. He was very interested, and even more so when he heard from Ram Dass about the adventure of the monkey on the roof. Ram Dass made for him a very clear picture of the attic and its bleakness — of the bare floor and broken plaster, the rusty, empty grate, and the hard, narrow bed.

12.15.oldText: “Carmichael,” he said to the father of the Large Family, after he had heard this description, “I wonder how many of the attics in this square are like that one, and how many wretched little servant girls sleep on such beds, while I toss on my down pillows, weighed down and tormented by wealth that is, most of it — not mine.”

12.16.oldText: “My dear fellow,” Mr. Carmichael answered cheerily, “the sooner you stop tormenting yourself, the better it will be for you. If you owned all the wealth of all the Indies, you could not set right all the discomforts in the world, and if you began to refurnish all the attics in this square, there would still be all the attics in all the other squares and streets to put in order. And there you are!”

12.17.oldText: Mr. Carrisford sat and bit his nails as he looked into the glowing bed of coals in the grate.

12.18.oldText: “Do you suppose,” he said slowly, after a pause, “do you think it is possible that the other child — the child I never stop thinking of, I believe — could be — could POSSIBLY be reduced to anything like the condition of the poor little soul next door?”

12.19.oldText: Mr. Carmichael looked at him uneasily. He knew that the worst thing the man could do for himself, for his sanity and his health, was to start thinking in this particular way about this particular subject.

12.20.oldText: “If the child at Madame Pascal's school in Paris was the one you are searching for,” he answered soothingly, “she would seem to be in the hands of people who can afford to take care of her. They adopted her because she had been the favourite companion of their little daughter, who died. They had no other children, and Madame Pascal said they were extremely well-to-do Russians.”

12.21.oldText: “And the wretched woman actually did not know where they had taken her!” exclaimed Mr. Carrisford.

12.23.oldText: “She was a shrewd, worldly Frenchwoman, and was clearly only too glad to get the child so comfortably off her hands when the father's death left her totally unprovided for. Women of her type do not trouble themselves about the futures of children who might prove burdens. The adopted parents apparently disappeared and left no trace.”

12.24.oldText: “But you say ‘IF the child was the one I am in search of.’ You say ‘if.’ We are not sure. There was a difference in the name.”

12.25.oldText: “Madame Pascal pronounced it as if it were Carew instead of Crewe — but that might just be a matter of pronunciation. The circumstances were curiously similar. An English officer in India had placed his motherless little girl at the school. He had died suddenly after losing his fortune.” Mr. Carmichael paused a moment, as if a new thought had occurred to him. “Are you SURE the child was left at a school in Paris? Are you sure it was Paris?”

12.26.oldText: “My dear fellow,” broke out Carrisford, with restless bitterness, “I am SURE of nothing. I never saw either the child or her mother. Ralph Crewe and I loved each other as boys, but we had not met since our school days, until we met in India. I was absorbed in the magnificent promise of the mines. He became absorbed too. The whole thing was so huge and glittering that we half lost our heads. When we met we scarcely spoke of anything else. I only knew that the child had been sent to school somewhere. I do not even remember now HOW I knew it.”

12.27.oldText: He was beginning to grow excited. He always became excited when his still weakened brain was stirred by memories of the catastrophes of the past.

12.28.oldText: Mr. Carmichael watched him anxiously. It was necessary to ask some questions, but they had to be put quietly and carefully.

12.29.oldText: “But you had reason to think the school WAS in Paris?”

12.30.oldText: “Yes,” was the answer, “because her mother was a Frenchwoman, and I had heard that she wished her child to be educated in Paris. It seemed only likely that she would be there.”

12.31.oldText: “Yes,” Mr. Carmichael said, “it seems more than probable.”

12.32.oldText: The Indian gentleman leaned forward and struck the table with a long, wasted hand.

12.33.oldText: “Carmichael,” he said, “I MUST find her. If she is alive, she is somewhere. If she is friendless and penniless, it is through my fault. How is a man to get back his nerve with a thing like that on his mind? This sudden change of luck at the mines has made realities of all our most fantastic dreams, and poor Crewe's child may be begging in the street!”

12.34.oldText: “No, no,” said Carmichael. “Try to be calm. Console yourself with the fact that when she is found, you have a fortune to hand over to her.”

12.35.oldText: “Why was I not man enough to stand my ground when things looked black?” Carrisford groaned in petulant misery. “I believe I should have stood my ground if I had not been responsible for other people's money as well as my own. Poor Crewe had put into the scheme every penny he owned. He trusted me — he LOVED me. And he died thinking I had ruined him — I — Tom Carrisford, who played cricket at Eton with him. What a villain he must have thought me!”

12.37.oldText: “I don't reproach myself because the speculation threatened to fail — I reproach myself for losing my courage. I ran away like a swindler and a thief, because I could not face my best friend and tell him I had ruined him and his child.”

12.38.oldText: The good-hearted father of the Large Family put his hand on his shoulder comfortingly.

12.39.oldText: “You ran away because your brain had given way under the strain of mental torture,” he said. “You were half delirious already. If you had not been, you would have stayed and fought it out. You were in a hospital, strapped down in bed, raving with brain fever, two days after you left the place. Remember that.”

12.40.oldText: Carrisford dropped his forehead in his hands.

12.41.oldText: “Good God! Yes,” he said. “I was driven mad with dread and horror. I had not slept for weeks. The night I staggered out of my house, all the air seemed full of hideous things mocking and mouthing at me.”

12.42.oldText: “That is explanation enough in itself,” said Mr. Carmichael. “How could a man on the verge of brain fever judge sanely!”

12.44.oldText: “And when I came back to consciousness, poor Crewe was dead — and buried. And I seemed to remember nothing. I did not remember the child for months and months. Even when I began to recall her existence, everything seemed in a sort of haze.”

12.45.oldText: He stopped a moment and rubbed his forehead. “It sometimes seems so now when I try to remember. Surely I must sometime have heard Crewe speak of the school she was sent to. Don't you think so?”

12.46.oldText: “He might not have spoken of it definitely. You never seem even to have heard her real name.”

12.47.oldText: “He used to call her by an odd pet name he had invented. He called her his ‘Little Missus.’ But the wretched mines drove everything else out of our heads. We talked of nothing else. If he spoke of the school, I forgot — I forgot. And now I shall never remember.”

12.48.oldText: “Come, come,” said Carmichael. “We shall find her yet. We will keep searching for Madame Pascal's good-natured Russians. She seemed to have a vague idea that they lived in Moscow. We will take that as a clue. I will go to Moscow.”

12.49.oldText: “If I were able to travel, I would go with you,” said Carrisford; “but I can only sit here wrapped in furs and stare at the fire. And when I look into it, I seem to see Crewe's gay young face gazing back at me. He looks as if he were asking me a question. Sometimes I dream of him at night, and he always stands before me and asks the same question in words. Can you guess what he says, Carmichael?”

12.50.oldText: Mr. Carmichael answered him in a rather low voice.

12.52.oldText: “He always says, ‘Tom, old man — Tom — where is the Little Missus?’” He caught at Carmichael's hand and clung to it. “I must be able to answer him — I must!” he said. “Help me to find her. Help me.”

12.53.oldText: On the other side of the wall, Sara was sitting in her garret talking to Melchisedec, who had come out for his evening meal.

12.54.oldText: “It has been hard to be a princess today, Melchisedec,” she said. “It has been harder than usual. It gets harder as the weather grows colder and the streets get more sloppy. When Lavinia laughed at my muddy skirt as I passed her in the hall, I thought of something to say all in a flash — and I only just stopped myself in time. You can't sneer back at people like that — if you are a princess. But you have to bite your tongue to hold yourself in. I bit mine. It was a cold afternoon, Melchisedec. And it's a cold night.”

12.55.oldText: Quite suddenly she put her black head down in her arms, as she often did when she was alone.

12.56.oldText: “Oh, papa,” she whispered, “what a long time it seems since I was your ‘Little Missus’!”

12.57.oldText: This was what happened that day on both sides of the wall.

13.0.oldText: The winter was a miserable one. There were days when Sara tramped through snow on her errands. There were worse days when the snow melted and mixed with mud to form slush. There were others when the fog was so thick that the streetlamps were lit all day, and London looked the way it had several years ago, on the afternoon when the cab had driven through the streets with Sara tucked up on its seat, leaning against her father's shoulder. On such days the windows of the house belonging to the Large Family always looked wonderfully cozy and inviting, and the study where the Indian gentleman sat glowed with warmth and rich color. But the attic was dismal beyond words. There were no longer any sunsets or sunrises to look at, and hardly ever any stars, it seemed to Sara. The clouds hung low over the skylight, and were either gray or mud-colored, or dropping heavy rain. At four o'clock in the afternoon, even when there was no special fog, the daylight was gone. If she needed to go to her attic for anything, Sara had to light a candle. The women in the kitchen were depressed, and that made them more bad-tempered than ever. Becky was driven like a little slave.

13.1.oldText: “If it weren't for you, miss,” she said hoarsely to Sara one night when she had crept into the attic, “if it weren't for you, an' the Bastille, an' bein' the prisoner in the next cell, I should die. That there does seem real now, doesn't it? The missus is more like the head jailer every day she lives. I can just see them big keys you say she carries. The cook, she's like one of the under-jailers. Tell me some more, please, miss—tell me about the underground passage we've dug under the walls.”

13.2.oldText: “I'll tell you something warmer,” Sara said with a shiver. “Get your coverlet and wrap it round you, and I'll get mine, and we will huddle close together on the bed, and I'll tell you about the tropical forest where the Indian gentleman's monkey used to live. When I see him sitting on the table near the window and looking out into the street with that sad expression, I always feel sure he is thinking about the tropical forest where he used to swing by his tail from coconut trees. I wonder who caught him, and if he left a family behind that had depended on him for coconuts.”

13.3.oldText: “That is warmer, miss,” Becky said gratefully, “but somehow even the Bastille is sort of heating when you start telling about it.”

13.4.oldText: “That is because it makes you think of something else,” Sara said, wrapping the coverlet round her until only her small dark face peeped out of it. “I've noticed this. What you have to do with your mind, when your body is miserable, is to make it think of something else.”

13.5.oldText: “Can you do it, miss?” Becky asked hesitantly, gazing at her with admiring eyes.

13.6.oldText: Sara knitted her brows for a moment.

13.7.oldText: “Sometimes I can and sometimes I can't,” she said firmly. “But when I can, I'm all right. And what I believe is that we always could—if we practiced enough. I've been practicing a good deal lately, and it's beginning to be easier than it used to be. When things are horrible—just horrible—I think as hard as ever I can about being a princess. I say to myself, ‘I am a princess, and I am a fairy one, and because I am a fairy nothing can hurt me or make me uncomfortable.’ You don't know how it makes you forget,” she added with a laugh.

13.8.oldText: She had many chances to make her mind think of something else, and many chances to prove to herself whether or not she was a princess. But one of the strongest tests she was ever put to came on a certain dreadful day which, she often thought afterward, would never quite fade out of her memory even in the years to come.

13.9.oldText: For several days it had rained without stopping. The streets were chilly and sloppy and full of dreary, cold mist. There was mud everywhere—sticky London mud—and over everything hung the heavy curtain of drizzle and fog. Of course there were several long and tiresome errands to be done—there always were on days like this—and Sara was sent out again and again, until her shabby clothes were damp through. The silly old feathers on her sad-looking hat were more bedraggled and ridiculous than ever, and her worn-out shoes were so wet that they could not hold any more water. On top of all that, she had been deprived of her dinner, because Miss Minchin had decided to punish her. She was so cold and hungry and tired that her face began to look pinched, and now and then some kind-hearted person passing her on the street glanced at her with sudden sympathy. But she did not know that. She hurried on, trying to make her mind think of something else. It was really very necessary. Her way of doing it was to “pretend” and “suppose” with all the strength she had left. But really this time it was harder than she had ever found it, and once or twice she thought it almost made her more cold and hungry instead of less so. But she stubbornly kept at it, and as the muddy water squelched through her broken shoes and the wind seemed to be trying to drag her thin jacket from her, she talked to herself as she walked, though she did not speak aloud or even move her lips.

13.10.oldText: “Suppose I had dry clothes on,” she thought. “Suppose I had good shoes and a long, thick coat and warm wool stockings and a whole umbrella. And suppose—suppose—just when I was near a baker's where they sold hot buns, I should find sixpence—which belonged to nobody. Suppose if I did, I should go into the shop and buy six of the hottest buns and eat them all without stopping.”

13.11.oldText: Some very odd things happen in this world sometimes.

13.12.oldText: It certainly was an odd thing that happened to Sara. She had to cross the street just when she was saying this to herself. The mud was awful—she almost had to wade through it. She picked her way as carefully as she could, but she could not save herself much. As she picked her way, though, she had to look down at her feet and the mud, and in looking down—just as she reached the pavement—she saw something shining in the gutter. It was actually a piece of silver—a tiny piece trodden upon by many feet, but still with enough spirit left in it to shine a little. Not quite a sixpence, but the next thing to it—a fourpenny piece.

13.13.oldText: In one second it was in her cold little red-and-blue hand.

13.14.oldText: “Oh,” she gasped, “it is true! It is true!”

13.15.oldText: And then, if you will believe me, she looked straight at the shop directly facing her. And it was a baker's shop, and a cheerful, plump, motherly woman with rosy cheeks was putting into the window a tray of delicious newly baked hot buns, fresh from the oven—large, plump, shiny buns, with currants in them.

13.16.oldText: It almost made Sara feel faint for a few seconds—the shock, and the sight of the buns, and the wonderful smells of warm bread floating up through the baker's cellar window.

13.17.oldText: She knew she did not need to hesitate to use the little piece of money. It had clearly been lying in the mud for some time, and its owner was completely lost in the stream of passing people who crowded and jostled each other all day long.

13.18.oldText: “But I'll go and ask the baker woman if she has lost anything,” she said to herself, rather faintly. So she crossed the pavement and put her wet foot on the step. As she did so she saw something that made her stop.

13.19.oldText: It was a little figure even more forlorn than herself—a little figure that was not much more than a bundle of rags, from which small, bare, red, muddy feet peeped out, only because the rags the owner was trying to cover them with were not long enough. Above the rags appeared a shock of tangled hair, and a dirty face with big, hollow, hungry eyes.

13.20.oldText: Sara knew they were hungry eyes the moment she saw them, and she felt a sudden rush of sympathy.

13.21.oldText: “This,” she said to herself, with a little sigh, “is one of the populace—and she is hungrier than I am.”

13.22.oldText: The child—this “one of the populace”—stared up at Sara, and shuffled herself aside a little so as to give her room to pass. She was used to being made to give room to everybody. She knew that if a policeman happened to see her, he would tell her to “move on.”

13.23.oldText: Sara clutched her little fourpenny piece and hesitated for a few seconds. Then she spoke to her.

13.25.oldText: The child shuffled herself and her rags a little more.

13.26.oldText: “Ain't I just?” she said in a hoarse voice. “Just ain't I?”

13.27.oldText: “Haven't you had any dinner?” Sara asked.

13.28.oldText: “No dinner,” the child said, even more hoarsely and shuffling more. “Nor no breakfast—nor no supper. No nothin'.”

13.30.oldText: “Dunno. Never got nothin' today—nowhere. I've asked an' asked.”

13.31.oldText: Just to look at her made Sara more hungry and faint. But those strange little thoughts were at work in her brain, and she was talking to herself, even though she was sick at heart.

13.32.oldText: “If I'm a princess,” she was saying, “if I'm a princess—when they were poor and driven from their thrones—they always shared—with the populace—if they met someone poorer and hungrier than themselves. They always shared. Buns are a penny each. If it had been sixpence, I could have eaten six. It won't be enough for either of us. But it will be better than nothing.”

13.33.oldText: “Wait a minute,” she said to the beggar child.

13.34.oldText: She went into the shop. It was warm and smelled delicious. The woman was just about to put some more hot buns into the window.

13.35.oldText: “Excuse me,” Sara said, “have you lost fourpence—a silver fourpence?” And she held the sad little piece of money out to her.

13.36.oldText: The woman looked at it, and then at her—at her intense little face and bedraggled, once fine clothes.

13.37.oldText: “Bless us, no,” she answered. “Did you find it?”

13.39.oldText: “Keep it, then,” the woman said. “It may have been there for a week, and goodness knows who lost it. You could never find out.”

13.40.oldText: “I know that,” Sara said, “but I thought I would ask you.”

13.41.oldText: “Not many would,” the woman said, looking puzzled and interested and good-natured all at once.

13.42.oldText: “Do you want to buy something?” she added, as she saw Sara glance at the buns.

13.43.oldText: “Four buns, please,” Sara said. “Those at a penny each.”

13.44.oldText: The woman went to the window and put some in a paper bag.

13.45.oldText: Sara noticed that she put in six.

13.46.oldText: “I said four, please,” she explained. “I have only fourpence.”

13.47.oldText: “I'll throw in two extra,” the woman said with her good-natured look. “I dare say you can eat them sometime. Aren't you hungry?”

13.48.oldText: A mist rose before Sara's eyes.

13.49.oldText: “Yes,” she answered. “I am very hungry, and I am much obliged to you for your kindness; and—” She was going to add, “there is a child outside who is hungrier than I am.” But just at that moment two or three customers came in at once, and each one seemed in a hurry, so she could only thank the woman again and go out.

13.50.oldText: The beggar girl was still huddled up in the corner of the step. She looked frightful in her wet and dirty rags. She was staring straight ahead with a dull look of suffering, and Sara saw her suddenly draw the back of her rough black hand across her eyes to rub away the tears that seemed to have surprised her by forcing their way from under her lids. She was muttering to herself.

13.51.oldText: Sara opened the paper bag and took out one of the hot buns, which had already warmed her own cold hands a little.

13.52.oldText: “See,” she said, putting the bun in the ragged lap, “this is nice and hot. Eat it, and you will not feel so hungry.”

13.53.oldText: The child started and stared up at her, as if such sudden, amazing good luck almost frightened her. Then she snatched up the bun and began to cram it into her mouth with great wolfish bites.

13.54.oldText: “Oh, my! Oh, my!” Sara heard her say hoarsely, in wild delight. “Oh my!”

13.55.oldText: Sara took out three more buns and put them down.

13.56.oldText: The sound in the hoarse, ravenous voice was awful.

13.57.oldText: “She is hungrier than I am,” she said to herself. “She's starving.” But her hand trembled when she put down the fourth bun. “I'm not starving,” she said—and she put down the fifth.

13.58.oldText: The little ravenous London savage was still snatching and devouring when Sara turned away. She was too hungry to give any thanks, even if she had ever been taught manners—which she had not. She was only a poor little wild animal.

13.60.oldText: When she reached the other side of the street, she looked back. The child had a bun in each hand and had stopped in the middle of a bite to watch her. Sara gave her a little nod, and the child, after another stare—a curious lingering stare—jerked her shaggy head in response, and until Sara was out of sight she did not take another bite or even finish the one she had begun.

13.61.oldText: At that moment the baker-woman looked out of her shop window.

13.62.oldText: “Well, I never!” she exclaimed. “If that young one hasn't given her buns to a beggar child! It wasn't because she didn't want them, either. Well, well, she looked hungry enough. I'd give something to know what she did it for.”

13.63.oldText: She stood behind her window for a few moments and pondered. Then her curiosity got the better of her. She went to the door and spoke to the beggar child.

13.64.oldText: “Who gave you those buns?” she asked her. The child nodded her head toward Sara's vanishing figure.

13.65.oldText: “What did she say?” the woman asked.

13.66.oldText: “Asked me if I was hungry,” replied the hoarse voice.

13.69.oldText: “And then she came in and got the buns, and gave them to you, did she?”

13.74.oldText: “Left just one for herself,” she said in a low voice. “And she could have eaten the whole six—I saw it in her eyes.”

13.75.oldText: She looked after the little bedraggled, far-away figure and felt more disturbed in her usually comfortable mind than she had felt for many a day.

13.76.oldText: “I wish she hadn't gone so quick,” she said. “I'm blessed if she shouldn't have had a dozen.” Then she turned to the child.

13.78.oldText: “I'm always hungry,” was the answer, “but it ain't as bad as it was.”

13.79.oldText: “Come in here,” the woman said, and she held the shop door open.

13.80.oldText: The child got up and shuffled in. To be invited into a warm place full of bread seemed an unbelievable thing. She did not know what was going to happen. She did not even care.

13.81.oldText: “Get yourself warm,” the woman said, pointing to a fire in the tiny back room. “And look here—when you are short of a bit of bread, you can come in here and ask for it. I'm blessed if I won't give it to you for that young one's sake.”

13.82.oldText: Sara found some comfort in her remaining bun. At least it was very hot, and it was better than nothing. As she walked along, she broke off small pieces and ate them slowly to make them last longer.

13.83.oldText: “Suppose it was a magic bun,” she said, “and a bite was as much as a whole dinner. I should be overeating myself if I went on like this.”

13.84.oldText: It was dark when she reached the square where the Select Seminary was. The lights in the houses were all on. The blinds were not yet drawn in the windows of the room where she nearly always caught glimpses of members of the Large Family. Often at this hour she could see the gentleman she called Mr. Montmorency sitting in a big chair, with a small swarm round him, talking, laughing, perching on the arms of his seat or on his knees, or leaning against them. This evening the swarm was around him, but he was not seated. On the contrary, there was a good deal of excitement going on. It was clear that a journey was about to be taken, and it was Mr. Montmorency who was to take it. A carriage stood before the door, and a big travel trunk had been strapped onto it. The children were dancing about, chattering and hanging on to their father. The pretty rosy mother was standing near him, talking as if she was asking final questions. Sara paused a moment to see the little ones lifted up and kissed, and the bigger ones bent over and kissed too.

13.85.oldText: “I wonder if he will stay away long,” she thought. “The trunk is rather big. Oh, dear, how they will miss him! I shall miss him myself—even though he doesn't know I am alive.”

13.86.oldText: When the door opened she moved away—remembering the sixpence—but she saw the traveler come out and stand against the background of the warmly lit hall, the older children still hovering about him.

13.87.oldText: “Will Moscow be covered with snow?” asked the little girl Janet. “Will there be ice everywhere?”

13.88.oldText: “Will you drive in a sleigh?” cried another. “Will you see the Czar?”

13.89.oldText: “I will write and tell you all about it,” he answered, laughing. “And I will send you pictures of Russian peasants and things. Run into the house. It is a horrible damp night. I would rather stay with you than go to Moscow. Good night! Good night, duckies! God bless you!” And he ran down the steps and jumped into the carriage.

13.90.oldText: “If you find the little girl, give her our love!” shouted Guy Clarence, jumping up and down on the doormat.

13.91.oldText: Then they went in and shut the door.

13.92.oldText: “Did you see,” Janet said to Nora as they went back to the room, “the little-girl-who-is-not-a-beggar was passing? She looked all cold and wet, and I saw her turn her head over her shoulder and look at us. Mamma says her clothes always look as if they had been given to her by someone quite rich—someone who only let her have them because they were too shabby to wear. The people at the school always send her out on errands on the worst days and nights there are.”

13.93.oldText: Sara crossed the square to Miss Minchin's area steps, feeling faint and shaky.

13.94.oldText: “I wonder who the little girl is,” she thought—“the little girl he is going to look for.”

13.95.oldText: And she went down the area steps, dragging her basket and finding it very heavy indeed, while the father of the Large Family drove quickly on his way to the station to take the train that was to carry him to Moscow, where he was to do his very best to search for the lost little daughter of Captain Crewe.

14.0.oldText: On this very afternoon, while Sara was out, a strange thing happened in the attic. Only Melchisedec saw and heard it; and he was so alarmed and confused that he scuttled back to his hole and hid there, really quaking and trembling as he peeped out cautiously and very carefully to watch what was going on.

14.1.oldText: The attic had been very still all day after Sara had left it in the early morning. The stillness had only been broken by the patter of rain on the slates and the skylight. Melchisedec had, in fact, found it rather dull. When the rain stopped pattering and perfect silence settled in, he decided to come out and look around, even though experience had taught him that Sara would not return for some time. He had been wandering and sniffing about, and had just found a totally unexpected and unexplained crumb left from his last meal, when his attention was caught by a sound on the roof. He stopped to listen with a fluttering heart. The sound suggested that something was moving on the roof. It was approaching the skylight; it reached the skylight. The skylight was being mysteriously opened. A dark face peered into the attic; then another face appeared behind it, and both looked in with signs of caution and interest. Two men were outside on the roof, and were silently preparing to enter through the skylight itself. One was Ram Dass and the other was a young man who was the Indian gentleman's secretary; but of course Melchisedec did not know this. He only knew that the men were invading the silence and privacy of the attic. As the one with the dark face let himself down through the opening with such lightness and skill that he did not make the slightest sound, Melchisedec turned tail and fled in a panic back to his hole. He was frightened to death. He had stopped being shy with Sara, and knew she would never throw anything but crumbs, and would never make any sound except the soft, low, coaxing whistle. But strange men were dangerous things to be near. He lay close and flat near the entrance of his home, just managing to peep through the crack with a bright, alarmed eye. How much he understood of the talk he heard, I am not in the least able to say; but even if he had understood it all, he would probably still have been greatly mystified.

14.2.oldText: The secretary, who was light and young, slipped through the skylight as silently as Ram Dass had done, and he caught a last glimpse of Melchisedec's vanishing tail.

14.3.oldText: “Was that a rat?” he asked Ram Dass in a whisper.

14.4.oldText: “Yes; a rat, Sahib,” answered Ram Dass, also whispering. “There are many in the walls.”

14.5.oldText: “Ugh!” exclaimed the young man. “It is a wonder the child is not terrified of them.”

14.6.oldText: Ram Dass made a gesture with his hands. He also smiled respectfully. He was in this place as the trusted spokesman for Sara, even though she had only spoken to him once.

14.7.oldText: “The child is the little friend of all things, Sahib,” he answered. “She is not like other children. I see her when she does not see me. I slip across the slates and look at her many nights to make sure she is safe. I watch her from my window when she does not know I am near. She stands on the table there and looks out at the sky as if it were speaking to her. The sparrows come at her call. The rat she has fed and tamed in her loneliness. The poor slave of the house comes to her for comfort. There is a little child who comes to her in secret; there is one older who worships her and would listen to her forever if she might. This I have seen when I have crept across the roof. By the mistress of the house—who is an evil woman—she is treated like an outcast; but she has the bearing of a child of royal blood!”

14.8.oldText: “You seem to know a great deal about her,” the secretary said.

14.9.oldText: “Each day of her life, I know,” answered Ram Dass. “Her going out I know, and her coming in; her sadness and her poor joys; her coldness and her hunger. I know when she is alone until midnight, learning from her books; I know when her secret friends sneak up to her and she is happier—as children can be, even in the middle of poverty—because they come and she may laugh and talk with them in whispers. If she were ill, I should know, and I would come and serve her if it could be done.”

14.10.oldText: “You are sure no one comes near this place but herself, and that she will not return and surprise us. She would be frightened if she found us here, and the Sahib Carrisford's plan would be spoiled.”

14.11.oldText: Ram Dass crossed silently to the door and stood close to it.

14.12.oldText: “No one comes up here but herself, Sahib,” he said. “She has gone out with her basket and may be gone for hours. If I stand here, I can hear any step before it reaches the last flight of the stairs.”

14.13.oldText: The secretary took a pencil and a notebook from his breast pocket.

14.14.oldText: “Keep your ears open,” he said; and he began to walk slowly and softly round the miserable little room, making rapid notes in his notebook as he looked at things.

14.15.oldText: First he went to the narrow bed. He pressed his hand on the mattress and let out an exclamation.

14.16.oldText: “As hard as a stone,” he said. “That will have to be changed some day when she is out. A special trip can be made to bring it across. It cannot be done tonight.” He lifted the cover and examined the one thin pillow.

14.17.oldText: “Coverlet dingy and worn, blanket thin, sheets patched and ragged,” he said. “What a bed for a child to sleep in—and in a house that calls itself respectable! There has not been a fire in that grate for many a day,” he added, glancing at the rusty fireplace.

14.18.oldText: “Never since I have seen it,” said Ram Dass. “The mistress of the house is not one who remembers that anyone other than herself might be cold.”

14.19.oldText: The secretary was writing quickly in his notebook. He looked up from it as he tore off a leaf and slipped it into his breast pocket.

14.20.oldText: “It is a strange way of doing the thing,” he said. “Who planned it?”

14.21.oldText: Ram Dass made a modestly apologetic bow.

14.22.oldText: “It is true that the first thought was mine, Sahib,” he said; “though it was nothing but a fancy. I am fond of this child; we are both lonely. It is her way to share her visions with her secret friends. Being sad one night, I lay close to the open skylight and listened. The vision she described told what this miserable room might be if it had comforts in it. She seemed to see it as she talked, and she grew cheered and warmed as she spoke. Then she came to this fancy; and the next day, the Sahib being ill and wretched, I told him of the thing to amuse him. It seemed then but a dream, but it pleased the Sahib. To hear of the child's doings entertained him. He became interested in her and asked questions. At last he began to please himself with the thought of making her visions into real things.”

14.23.oldText: “You think that it can be done while she sleeps? Suppose she woke up,” the secretary suggested; and it was clear that whatever the plan referred to was, it had caught and pleased his fancy as well as the Sahib Carrisford's.

14.24.oldText: “I can move as if my feet were of velvet,” Ram Dass replied; “and children sleep soundly—even the unhappy ones. I could have entered this room in the night many times, and without making her turn on her pillow. If the other bearer passes the things to me through the window, I can do it all and she will not stir. When she wakes she will think a magician has been here.”

14.25.oldText: He smiled as if his heart warmed under his white robe, and the secretary smiled back at him.

14.26.oldText: “It will be like a story from the Arabian Nights,” he said. “Only an Easterner could have planned it. It does not belong to London fogs.”

14.27.oldText: They did not stay very long, to the great relief of Melchisedec, who, since he probably did not understand their conversation, found their movements and whispers ominous. The young secretary seemed interested in everything. He wrote down things about the floor, the fireplace, the broken footstool, the old table, the walls—which last he touched with his hand again and again, seeming much pleased when he found that a number of old nails had been driven in various places.

14.28.oldText: “You can hang things on them,” he said.

14.30.oldText: “Yesterday, when she was out,” he said, “I came in, bringing with me small, sharp nails which can be pressed into the wall without blows from a hammer. I placed many in the plaster where I may need them. They are ready.”

14.31.oldText: The Indian gentleman's secretary stood still and looked round him as he pushed his notebook back into his pocket.

14.32.oldText: “I think I have made enough notes; we can go now,” he said. “The Sahib Carrisford has a warm heart. It is a thousand pities that he has not found the lost child.”

14.33.oldText: “If he should find her, his strength would be restored to him,” said Ram Dass. “His God may lead her to him yet.”

14.34.oldText: Then they slipped through the skylight as silently as they had entered it. And after he was quite sure they had gone, Melchisedec was greatly relieved, and after a few minutes felt it was safe to come out of his hole again and scuffle about in the hope that even such alarming human beings as these might have happened to carry crumbs in their pockets and dropped one or two of them.

15.27.oldText: Melchisedec had come out of his hole as if he had been listening for her footstep. Sara was quite sure he knew it. He came forward with an affectionate, expectant expression as Sara put her hand in her pocket and turned it inside out, shaking her head.

19.0.oldText: Never had such joy filled the nursery of the Large Family. Never had they imagined such delights as came from getting to know the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar. The mere fact of her sufferings and adventures made her a priceless treasure. Everyone wanted to be told over and over again the things that had happened to her. When you sat by a warm fire in a big, glowing room, it was quite delightful to hear how cold an attic could be. It must be admitted that the attic was rather enjoyed, and that its coldness and bareness sank into insignificance when Melchisedec was remembered, and you heard about the sparrows and the things you could see if you climbed onto the table and stuck your head and shoulders out of the skylight.

19.1.oldText: Of course, the thing they loved best was the story of the banquet and the dream that came true. Sara told it for the first time the day after she had been found. Several members of the Large Family came to take tea with her, and as they sat or curled up on the hearth-rug, she told the story in her own way, and the Indian gentleman listened and watched her. When she had finished, she looked up at him and put her hand on his knee.

19.2.oldText: “That is my part,” she said. “Now won't you tell your part of it, Uncle Tom?” He had asked her always to call him “Uncle Tom.” “I don't know your part yet, and it must be beautiful.”

19.3.oldText: So he told them how, when he sat alone, ill and dull and irritable, Ram Dass had tried to distract him by describing the people walking by, and there was one child who passed more often than anyone else. He had begun to be interested in her—partly perhaps because he was thinking a great deal about a little girl, and partly because Ram Dass had been able to relate the incident of his visit to the attic chasing the monkey. He had described its cheerless look, and the bearing of the child, who seemed as if she were not of the class of those treated as drudges and servants. Bit by bit, Ram Dass had made discoveries about the wretchedness of her life. He had found out how easy it was to climb across the few yards of roof to the skylight, and this fact had been the beginning of all that followed.

19.4.oldText: “Sahib,” he had said one day, “I could cross the slates and make the child a fire when she is out on some errand. When she returned, wet and cold, to find it blazing, she would think a magician had done it.”

19.5.oldText: The idea had been so fanciful that Mr. Carrisford's sad face had lit up with a smile, and Ram Dass had been so filled with delight that he had expanded on it and explained to his master how simple it would be to do many other things. He had shown a childlike pleasure and inventiveness, and the preparations for carrying out the plan had filled many a day with interest that would otherwise have dragged wearily. On the night of the ruined banquet, Ram Dass had kept watch, all his packages ready in the attic that was his own. The person who was to help him had waited with him, as interested as he was in the strange adventure. Ram Dass had been lying flat on the slates, looking in at the skylight, when the banquet had come to its disastrous end. He had been sure of how deeply Sara was sleeping in her exhaustion. Then, with a dark lantern, he had crept into the room, while his companion remained outside and handed the things in to him. When Sara had stirred even faintly, Ram Dass had closed the lantern-slide and lain flat on the floor. These and many other exciting things the children found out by asking a thousand questions.

19.6.oldText: “I am so glad,” Sara said. “I am so glad it was you who were my friend!”

19.7.oldText: There were never such friends as these two became. Somehow, they seemed to suit each other in a wonderful way. The Indian gentleman had never had a companion he liked quite as much as he liked Sara. Within a month, he was, as Mr. Carmichael had predicted, a new man. He was always amused and interested, and he began to find an actual pleasure in owning the wealth he had imagined he hated being burdened with. There were so many charming things to plan for Sara. There was a little joke between them that he was a magician, and one of his pleasures was inventing things to surprise her. She found beautiful new flowers growing in her room, whimsical little gifts tucked under pillows, and once, as they sat together in the evening, they heard the scratch of a heavy paw on the door. When Sara went to find out what it was, there stood a great dog—a splendid Russian boarhound—with a grand silver and gold collar bearing an inscription. “I am Boris,” it read. “I serve the Princess Sara.”

19.8.oldText: There was nothing the Indian gentleman loved more than remembering the little princess in rags and tatters. The afternoons when the Large Family, or Ermengarde and Lottie, gathered to celebrate together were very delightful. But the hours when Sara and the Indian gentleman sat alone reading or talking had a special charm of their own. During those hours many interesting things happened.

19.9.oldText: One evening, Mr. Carrisford, looking up from his book, noticed that his companion had not stirred for some time, but sat gazing into the fire.

19.11.oldText: Sara looked up, with a bright color on her cheek.

19.12.oldText: “I was supposing,” she said. “I was remembering that hungry day, and a child I saw.”

19.13.oldText: “But there were a great many hungry days,” said the Indian gentleman, with a rather sad tone in his voice. “Which hungry day was it?”

19.14.oldText: “I forgot you didn't know,” said Sara. “It was the day the dream came true.”

19.15.oldText: Then she told him the story of the bun shop, and the fourpence she picked up out of the sloppy mud, and the child who was hungrier than she was. She told it quite simply, and in as few words as possible; but somehow the Indian gentleman found it necessary to shade his eyes with his hand and look down at the carpet.

19.16.oldText: “And I was supposing a kind of plan,” she said when she had finished. “I was thinking I would like to do something.”

19.17.oldText: “What was it?” said Mr. Carrisford in a low tone. “You may do anything you like, princess.”

19.18.oldText: “I was wondering,” Sara hesitated—“you know, you say I have so much money—I was wondering if I could go to see the bun-woman, and tell her that if hungry children come and sit on the steps, or look in at the window—particularly on those dreadful days—she could just call them in and give them something to eat, and send the bills to me. Could I do that?”

19.19.oldText: “You shall do it tomorrow morning,” said the Indian gentleman.

19.20.oldText: “Thank you,” said Sara. “You see, I know what it is to be hungry, and it is very hard when you cannot even pretend it away.”

19.21.oldText: “Yes, yes, my dear,” said the Indian gentleman. “Yes, yes, it must be. Try to forget it. Come and sit on this footstool near my knee, and only remember you are a princess.”

19.22.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara, smiling; “and I can give buns and bread to the populace.” And she went and sat on the stool, and the Indian gentleman (he sometimes liked her to call him that, too) drew her small dark head down on his knee and stroked her hair.

19.23.oldText: The next morning, Miss Minchin, looking out of her window, saw the things she perhaps least enjoyed seeing. The Indian gentleman's carriage, with its tall horses, drew up before the door of the next house, and its owner and a little figure, warm in soft, rich furs, came down the steps to get into it. The little figure was a familiar one, and reminded Miss Minchin of days in the past. It was followed by another familiar sight—one she found very irritating. It was Becky, who, in the role of delighted attendant, always accompanied her young mistress to her carriage, carrying wraps and belongings. Already Becky had a pink, round face.

19.24.oldText: A little later the carriage drew up before the door of the baker's shop, and its occupants got out, oddly enough, just as the bun-woman was putting a tray of steaming-hot buns into the window.

19.25.oldText: When Sara entered the shop, the woman turned and looked at her, and, leaving the buns, came and stood behind the counter. For a moment she looked at Sara very hard indeed, and then her good-natured face lit up.

19.26.oldText: “I'm sure I remember you, miss,” she said. “And yet—”

19.27.oldText: “Yes,” said Sara. “Once you gave me six buns for fourpence, and—”

19.28.oldText: “And you gave five of them to a beggar child,” the woman broke in. “I've always remembered it. I couldn't make it out at first.” She turned to the Indian gentleman and spoke her next words to him. “I beg your pardon, sir, but there aren't many young people who notice a hungry face the way she did; and I've thought of it many a time. Excuse the liberty, miss”—to Sara—“but you look rosier and—well, better than you did that—that—”

19.29.oldText: “I am better, thank you,” said Sara. “And—I am much happier—and I have come to ask you to do something for me.”

19.30.oldText: “Me, miss!” exclaimed the bun-woman, smiling cheerfully. “Why, bless you! Yes, miss. What can I do?”

19.31.oldText: And then Sara, leaning on the counter, made her little proposal about the dreadful days and the hungry waifs and the buns.

19.32.oldText: The woman watched her, and listened with an astonished face.

19.33.oldText: “Why, bless me!” she said again when she had heard it all. “It'll be a pleasure to me to do it. I am a working woman myself and cannot afford to do much on my own, and there's plenty of trouble on every side; but, if you'll excuse me, I'm bound to say I've given away many a bit of bread since that wet afternoon, just from thinking of you—and how wet and cold you were, and how hungry you looked; and yet you gave away your hot buns as if you were a princess.”

19.34.oldText: The Indian gentleman smiled at this without meaning to, and Sara smiled a little, too, remembering what she had said to herself when she put the buns down on the ravenous child's ragged lap.

19.35.oldText: “She looked so hungry,” she said. “She was even hungrier than I was.”

19.36.oldText: “She was starving,” said the woman. “Many's the time she's told me of it since—how she sat there in the wet, and felt as if a wolf was tearing at her poor young insides.”

19.37.oldText: “Oh, have you seen her since then?” exclaimed Sara. “Do you know where she is?”

19.38.oldText: “Yes, I do,” answered the woman, smiling more good-naturedly than ever. “Why, she's in that back room there, miss, and has been for a month. She's going to turn out a decent, well-meaning girl, and she's such a help to me in the shop and in the kitchen as you'd scarcely believe, knowing how she's lived.”

19.39.oldText: She stepped to the door of the little back parlor and spoke; and the next minute a girl came out and followed her behind the counter. And there she actually was—the beggar-child, clean and neatly clothed, and looking as if she had not been hungry for a long time. She looked shy, but she had a nice face, now that she was no longer wild, and the savage look had gone from her eyes. She knew Sara in an instant, and stood and looked at her as if she could never look enough.

19.40.oldText: “You see,” said the woman, “I told her to come when she was hungry, and that when she came I'd give her odd jobs to do. And I found she was willing, and somehow I got to like her; and the end of it was, I've given her a place and a home, and she helps me, and behaves well, and is as thankful as a girl can be. Her name's Anne. She has no other.”

19.41.oldText: The children stood and looked at each other for a few minutes; and then Sara took her hand out of her muff and held it out across the counter, and Anne took it, and they looked straight into each other's eyes.

19.42.oldText: “I am so glad,” Sara said. “And I have just thought of something. Perhaps Mrs. Brown will let you be the one to give the buns and bread to the children. Perhaps you would like to do it because you know what it is to be hungry, too.”

19.44.oldText: And, somehow, Sara felt as if she understood her, though Anne said so little, and only stood still and looked and looked after her as she went out of the shop with the Indian gentleman, and they got into the carriage and drove away.
